World.title: Are hacks of U.S. water facilities a new front in the Iran war?
World.content:
Are hacks of U.S. water facilities a new front in the Iran war?

toggle caption Ellen Schmidt/AP

On a recent Monday morning in Braham, Minn., a local water operator made an unsettling discovery — the pump at the treatment plant wasn't working, threatening the flow of water to people's homes.

While investigating the root cause, crews took the plant offline, and the city urged Braham's 1,700 or so residents to conserve water while they drew on a backup supply stored in a local tank.

It only took a couple of hours for workers to restore the flow after taking manual control of the pump. The self-proclaimed homemade pie capital of Minnesota still hosted its annual Pie Day celebration at the Park Cafe just days later.

Sponsor Message

But what Braham officials quickly learned, after connecting with Minnesota state IT teams, was that they were not alone in the outages. The cause was a "coordinated cyberattack" against industrial technology nationwide, and cybersecurity experts and federal officials suspected Iran may be to blame.

It's nothing new. Adversaries, including Iran, have been targeting U.S. critical infrastructure for years, to steal data or cause disruptions. Once inside, they can ransom the data to make money or threaten access to and trust in critical resources, from water and power to transportation and their bank accounts. "Everything's connected to the internet in one way or another," Nate George, the mayor of Braham, told NPR in an interview. "It's not Braham in particular that's being targeted. It's the internet access points and the vulnerable technology," George, a U.S. Air Force reservist, continued.

While the hackers failed to compromise the water supply, they succeeded in inspiring headlines and provoking uncertainty. And the scope, scale and real-world impacts of the attacks, like the one in Braham, have been remarkable even to the experts.

"I can't recall a time when there's been this many targets at once with operational impact," said Rob Lee, the co-founder and CEO of Dragos, a cybersecurity firm focused on industrial technology. Lee told NPR he's aware of victims of this recent spate of attacks outside the water sector, as critical infrastructure operators tend to rely on the same technology. It's something Lee has been warning about for years. "This is pretty significant," Lee said.

Sponsor Message

Local and federal officials are looking to get their arms around what happened, help critical infrastructure operators secure their systems, reassure the public and prepare for the future for the more than 150,000 water and wastewater treatment systems in the U.S. — because the next wave of attacks could be worse.

"It appears this is a shot across the bow from Iran," Jake Braun, the former White House acting principal deputy national cyber director during the Biden administration, told NPR.

The timeline

Between July 26 and July 28, several local authorities in Minnesota let citizens know about problems at community water plants from Braham to Maple Plain, Minn., where officials declared a brief state of emergency before determining that "the immediate threat to public health, safety and welfare had been addressed."

Cities and towns across the country began to join their ranks. In Clayton County outside Atlanta, local officials issued a brief "boil water" advisory after a pump station failure was detected in the middle of the night. There were other outages in New Jersey and Michigan.

A cybersecurity information-sharing organization for the water sector, WaterISAC, was quick to convene a call for its 400 or so members across community water systems to disseminate intelligence from the federal government about the attacks. The EPA followed up with a publicly available webinar "to discuss an urgent operational matter dealing with cyber threats to the water sector."

The FBI then confirmed that at least seven states suffered similar attacks on water and wastewater facilities. Their investigation is ongoing.

The scope and scale could be much larger. Beyond Lee of Dragos mentioning victims outside the water sector, one state IT official who requested anonymity because they weren't authorized to comment on ongoing investigations, said there's still concern about the transportation and energy sectors being impacted by these attacks.

Sponsor Message

"I think that we have to assume that this attack is national in scope," said Braun, now the executive director of the Cyber Policy Initiative at the University of Chicago.

Ties to Iran

The U.S. government hasn't officially said yet who they think is responsible for the latest attacks on the water sector.

But it wouldn't be the first time nation-states have disrupted critical services for geopolitical reasons. Starting in 2015, Russia notably launched a series of cyberattacks on Ukrainian power grids, plunging residents into darkness before ever launching a full-scale invasion.

Iranian-linked hackers have gone after U.S. power and water before.

For example, in 2023, an Iranian-linked hacktivist group broke into and defaced industrial machines in a water facility in Aliquippa, Pa. The machines, some of whose components were made in Israel, were manipulated to display anti-Israel messages during the war between Israel and Hamas.

The Department of Homeland Security's Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency has published a detailed advisory about Iranian-linked hackers looking for vulnerabilities in industrial machines like those found in the water sector. That advisory first came out in April, and the authors updated it just days before this recent spate of attacks.

Michael Crean of cybersecurity firm SonicWall tells NPR that his company has seen a recent "spike" in bad actors "scanning" the internet for vulnerable devices, "trying to find potential weaknesses out there and see how they can exploit it." He said the team saw a similar spike in March before hackers with ties to Iran compromised American medical technology company Stryker, which resulted in data destruction.

"We're seeing somebody run their proof of concept," Crean said. "You know, what is it that you can do to … scare the American people? Water is one of those things," he said. "It's a necessity of life."

Sponsor Message

Neither the Iranian government nor the well-known Iranian hacktivists groups, including one called Cyber Av3ngers, the group linked to the Aliquippa water attacks, has taken credit for the recent wave of water attacks.

However, one cybersecurity expert who requested anonymity to discuss sensitive information told NPR there's intelligence linking the recent activity to the Iranian Revolutionary Guard Corps. "It was opportunistic, but was almost certainly a result of the war," the expert told NPR.

Braun, the former White House acting principal deputy national cyber director, has been working with hacking conference DEF CON and the National Rural Water Association to pilot a program called Project Franklin, bringing expert volunteers to rural water facilities to prepare for attacks just like this.

During an interview with NPR, he said there are several reasons Iran might want to launch these attacks beyond scaring the average American.

"Iran is targeting three things," said Braun. "Number one, it's showing the administration they can shut off water to our military assets … then, it's showing they can shut off the water to a key economic asset, our data centers," he said, referring to the engine behind frontier AI technology.

"Finally, it's in the middle of a war that the country is deeply divided over," Braun said. "It's telling the administration that they can undermine trust from the U.S. population that the U.S. government is capable of providing even basic services like water."

The view from local communities

Parts of the water industry have already been thinking about this problem. Last September, NPR interviewed Chris Hughes, one of two water and wastewater operators in Cavendish, Vt., who was part of Braun's pilot program. "It's scary that I'm the only door between you know, the Iranians, and our water system," Hughes told NPR.

Industrial operators like Hughes deal with all kinds of challenges, from storms and natural disasters to technical failures and squirrels chewing through wires. Experts like Hughes say it might be difficult for bad actors to actually "poison" the water remotely. But talking to cybersecurity experts opened his mind to all kinds of possibilities, like a hacker causing a pipe to explode by fluctuating the water pressure.

Sponsor Message

There's a lot of damage hackers could do, particularly if industrial machines are connected to the internet. Technology helps some operators monitor their systems remotely and become more efficient, but it can expose insecure devices to bad actors a world away.

"I've been in the field for 28 years, I love technology," said Brandon Huston of the Minnesota Wastewater Operators Association. "But I purposefully have not put that into my wastewater system," he continued. He said it would be too expensive in time, money, and expertise to keep those systems updated and secure. "Every city's got vulnerabilities," he explained.

Securing critical infrastructure is a unique challenge, because industries from water to power rely on the same aging, specialized technology that can't easily be replaced, patched, or secured, explains Patrick Gillespie, a security expert who specializes in what's called operational technology at GuidePoint Security.

Operational technology, or OT, monitors and controls physical processes in the real world, rather than software which runs virtual programs like email or word processing. "This technology is decades old," Gillespie said.

The water sector is no different.

"The equipment that opens valves and doses chemicals runs on small industrial computers," explained Mike Searight, the former chief information officer for the city of Waco, Texas and adviser for cybersecurity firm Elisity. These devices "can't be updated on demand," he said, "because the manufacturer has to certify the fix, [and] you may have to take the plant offline. Sometimes, no fix exists."

"Water isn't data. Breach a billing system and it costs money … breach a treatment plant and people get sick, or untreated sewage ends up in a river," Searight said.

What comes next

During this latest series of attacks on the water sector, bad actors appeared to go after low-hanging fruit. They targeted devices that were exposed to the open internet with no additional protections, devices whose default username and password were never changed, for example, information that's often leaked online and is easy to find or guess.

Sponsor Message

There are things operators can do to prevent these basic attacks, like changing the default credentials, taking their industrial machines offline, disconnecting industrial machines from the rest of their business networks, and installing strong access controls and firewalls.

But future attacks might not be so easy to detect, stop, and recover from.

U.S. national security officials have for years been warning about the threat posed by a Chinese-linked hacking group they call Volt Typhoon, a stealthy actor that's been burrowing into U.S. critical infrastructure and hiding there for years, maintaining that access to potentially wreak havoc in the event of a conflict like a Chinese invasion of Taiwan.

It's something Braham Mayor George says he's thinking about, using the skills he's learned in strategic planning in the U.S. Air Force Reserve.

"Chinese military officers have written playbooks about this," he said. "It's called unrestricted warfare…[It's] attacking the electrical grid, shutting down street lights, shutting down airports, things of that nature. It's all meant to not necessarily cause damage…but panic, or hype, or whatever's going to distract the government from what it's trying to do overseas," George said.

The recent attacks on the water sector could serve as motivation to prepare for the worst-case scenario.

"There's nothing that we can do to stop the threat actors from approaching and targeting assets in America any more than we can mitigate or stop a hurricane," said Kevin Morley, the head of federal relations for the American Water Works Association, or the AWWA, during an interview with NPR. "So we manage vulnerabilities and consequences … our ability to recover and respond to it will improve with time."

He said the quick response to the recent spate of attacks demonstrated the power of timely information sharing across federal, private and state and local partners. But the water sector needs more resources to improve its security baseline. In a letter to Congress after the nationwide attacks, the AWWA called for increased federal funding for cybersecurity across the sector.

Sponsor Message

More water operators could take advantage of intelligence sharing from WaterISAC, as the organization is working with the National Rural Water Association to make it easier and more affordable – particularly for those who serve under 10,000 people. "We're looking for new members to join, to be able to get the information from us before they see it in the news," Jennifer Lyn Walker, the director for Infrastructure CyberDefense at WaterISAC told NPR.

And Braun and his partners on Project Franklin are launching a new project called the Water Watch Center to give small utilities more support. Braun tells NPR their goal is to distribute resources through managed service providers, the third-party companies that already provide security solutions to the sector. They're also working with Vanderbilt University on a project funded by DARPA, the Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency, a wing of the Pentagon that supports innovative defense research, to train AI agents to defend operational technology in the water sector from attackers in real time.

A question of federal leadership

Despite these efforts nationwide to get the right tools and education into the hands of water operators, the scale of the problem is staggering.

NPR reached out to representatives from state IT systems and cybersecurity and emergency response teams across the country. While not every office responded, a common theme of conversation emerged.

They say there's still a lot of work to be done to get visibility into local systems and hunt for hackers, and the chronically underfunded water sector in particular doesn't have the resources or the expertise to do it on their own.

Meanwhile, that problem has only gotten more challenging to deal with after the Trump administration slashed the federal cybersecurity workforce in a sweeping effort to reduce the size of the federal bureaucracy.

"California avoided an impact in this instance, but that should not create a false sense of security," wrote a spokesperson for the California Governor's Office of Emergency Services in response to questions from NPR. "Federal cuts to the nation's cybersecurity workforce and critical programs have weakened the partnerships, threat intelligence, and technical support that help protect essential services across the country," they concluded.

Sponsor Message

Braun tells NPR that ultimately, in order for efforts like Project Franklin to succeed at scale, there will need to be federal funding. "We can't fund it with philanthropy forever," he said. "We're designing it so the federal government can step in and fund it to deliver security everywhere."

Lee of Dragos thinks it will take more than a devastating cyberattack as motivation to solve this problem, given the number of times the sector has been targeted already.

"I think it's going to require a fully appreciated stance by senior government officials that we need to lead the discussion, regardless of local politics. And that's going to be hard," he said.

"How do you get out in front of people who are already upset about data centers, price raises, and feeling left out of an economy in a country that doesn't feel like it's for everybody … and say, hey, by the way, China, Russia, and Iran, they want to hurt your kids. We're going to ask you to raise your electric bill by ten cents, your water bill by 15 cents, and we're going to modernize our infrastructure and try to take care of people. That's hard," Lee said.

"But until that level of leadership is taking place, I don't think another attack is going to get us there."

World.title: Here's how gyms, salons and ice cream are changing America's Main Streets
World.content:
Here's how gyms, salons and ice cream are changing America's Main Streets

toggle caption Thalia Juarez for NPR

Change sprawls constantly across the storefronts on the postcard streets of downtown Ridgewood, New Jersey.

The big avenue, East Ridgewood, cuts across streets called Walnut, Chestnut and Oak, and then abuts the train station that connects this commuter suburb to New York City. It's a town where anything is reachable within five, 10 minutes of driving, and its center is the proverbial Main Street.

"Ridgewood has always been known as the place to go shopping," says Joan Groome, who has lived here since 1968, when she opened a ski shop above a family-run store selling gifts and art.

Sponsor Message

Over the years, Groome watched a wave of big-box chains sweep through Ridgewood and then a wave of banks. Local retail like hers strived and survived or went under; doors have shut on a beloved stationery store, a family-owned pharmacy, a hardware shop.

toggle caption Thalia Juarez for NPR

Now a new shift is reshaping this downtown, as it has many around the U.S.: Stores that sell things are giving way to shops that sell services — spas, gyms, restaurants.

"We have now 11 barbershops in town," says Groome, now the executive director of the Ridgewood Chamber of Commerce. Around her, on just this one block, three ice cream cafés have opened, with a milkshake shop opening soon.

Last year marked the first time that the majority of U.S. retail space was leased to tenants selling services rather than goods, according to real estate data firm CoStar. This change is a response to changing spending habits, and it is shaking up malls, suburban shopping hubs and Main Streets nationwide.

toggle caption Thalia Juarez for NPR

A long-term trend at play

This year, in the 20 biggest metropolitan areas, CoStar data shows retail tenants declining for the third year in a row, while personal services and entertainment are ballooning: escape rooms and virtual golfing, medical spas and Pilates studios.

Sponsor Message

"Over the very long term, consumers have switched a lot of spending from retail goods to services in terms of share of wallet," says John Mercer, who tracks the state of retail at the analytics firm Coresight Research. "We think that that kind of long-term pattern will continue."

toggle caption Thalia Juarez for NPR

This shift was temporarily interrupted by the lockdowns of the coronavirus pandemic but has since roared back. And it's generally fueled by the wealthier spenders, though Mercer says surveys also suggest that some people choose to trade down to cheaper goods to redirect that saved money to services, for outings and experiences.

Much of the change is driven by what's on trend: wellness, beauty, fitness. And, of course, online shopping plays a huge role: When any purchase is a click away, people who physically go out to shop are often looking for more — for fun, an activity.

As Groome puts it: "You can't stroll Amazon."

toggle caption Thalia Juarez for NPR

Math is different for a mall vs. downtown

The building where Groome once had her ski shop is now a sushi spot. Her old bank — complete with the preserved vault and deposit boxes — is an Italian-inspired restaurant with a rooftop bar. Plenty of Ridgewood stores still sell things — clothes, shoes, home decor, antiques — but there are also over a hundred eateries, dozens of coffee shops, spas, salons, a stretching studio.

A trendy bakery recently opened across the street from Bookends, a small bookstore with a basement for book signings, which has been open since the 1980s. Store manager David Logan says the new neighbor has brought him new business.

toggle caption Thalia Juarez for NPR

"People walk out of there, and I've got my door open, so they see we're open," he says. Many leave the café straight for Bookends, he says. Often, it's mothers with little children, who linger in the kids section with activity books and Legos.

Sponsor Message

This is how the shift toward more services has played out in some of the busier malls. Shopping centers have been adding arcades, gyms and even health clinics as a way to draw people more regularly. But the math is less straightforward for downtowns, where a new eatery or gym tends to replace a shop, so more services often mean fewer shops.

"Because there's not as much retail," Logan says, "people are basically coming in just to go to the restaurant, and they may not necessarily walk around town."

toggle caption Thalia Juarez for NPR

Can't stroll down Instagram either

A few doors down, behind the counter of her jewelry store, Gina Jeon is also conflicted.

"I wonder if a town changing from beautiful boutique shops to more food and services — I wonder if that enriches the value of the town or takes away from it," she says.

Jeon's shop, Hot Jewelry Box, is an explosion of crystals and gemstones, silver and gold. She custom-makes jewelry by hand, letting shoppers pick their designs, and rearranges a section of the store every day — trying to give people reasons to visit, in person, again and again.

Jeon thinks more beautiful shops get people to shop more, while more restaurants don't. As she talks, she's hooking a charm onto a beaded chain for shopper Kate Ulrich, who's here for the second time in two days, to buy a green-and-red version of the necklace she'd previously bought in blue, green and white.

toggle caption Thalia Juarez for NPR

"I just like it because you can kind of mix and match your own, and you don't have to pay these like crazy internet prices that we're all duped into paying," Ulrich says. "It's like they just upcharge everything on Instagram because you see it, you love it, you have to have it."

Ulrich grew up down the highway and came to Jeon's shop as a child, when the store first opened two decades ago. Now she drives a half hour to Ridgewood to see her sister, who recently moved here with family, and they do exactly what local shop owners hope.

Sponsor Message

"It's fun to kind of walk the stroller up and down the street," Ulrich says. "You can kind of peer into everywhere because … it's something to do."

They snack and shop, buying things and little treats along the way — maybe some of that endlessly available ice cream — strolling, which you cannot do on Instagram either.

World.title: Nuclear power push ramps up uranium mill — and tribal health concerns
World.content:
Nuclear power push ramps up uranium mill — and tribal health concerns

toggle caption EcoFlight

WHITE MESA, Utah — On a hot April day, Malcolm Lehi maneuvered his Jeep Wrangler over a rough dirt road. He drove past junipers and sagebrush in search of Entrance Spring on land long connected to his tribe, the Ute Mountain Ute.

The cool, mossy spring lies just across the highway from White Mesa Mill, the nation's only remaining conventional uranium mill, which produces yellowcake for nuclear power fuel.

For decades, the mill has sparked debate over whether radioactive contamination threatens human health by getting into the water and the air. Concerns run especially deep in the White Mesa Ute Community, where Lehi and about 200 members of his tribe live some 5 miles south of the facility.

Sponsor Message

State regulators and the company that owns the mill contend that any pollution associated with it is contained. That's little consolation to nearby tribal members, who — aware of uranium's deadly legacy across the Colorado Plateau — have raised questions about the potential spread of toxic waste. Many won't drink the local water, relying on bottled water instead.

Now the tribe's concerns have taken on new urgency as the U.S. pushes to revive domestic uranium production. A federal law, passed in 2024, bans imports of Russian uranium by 2028, increasing pressure to develop domestic fuel supplies. President Trump set a goal to quadruple U.S. nuclear energy capacity by 2050. He issued orders to prioritize mining on federal lands and fast-track approval of mining projects. The Velvet-Wood uranium mine in Utah, for instance, zipped through federal environmental review in 11 days, to the dismay of local tribes who were given one week to offer input.

Trump's goal of quadrupling nuclear power capacity will be hard to meet, because it would require constructing more reactors — which are difficult to build and often meet local opposition, said David Hart, a senior fellow for climate and energy at the Council on Foreign Relations. But data centers and rising electricity demand have intensified interest in nuclear power as a low-carbon energy source, he said. And more states are opening the door to it.

Sponsor Message

So the effort to obtain the key ingredient, uranium, is underway.

Tension at the White Mesa Mill

The White Mesa Mill, built in 1980 near what is now the Bears Ears National Monument in southeastern Utah, is a focal point of this latest uranium boom — and the tensions between local tribal concerns and national economic interests.

Increased demand draws a steady flow of trucks carrying uranium ore to the mill from regional mines, including one near the Grand Canyon where the Havasupai Tribe lives. That ore is trucked through the Navajo Nation. And the mill plans to expand its waste storage, as well.

A former tribal councilmember, Lehi is part of a growing opposition that includes members of the Havasupai and Navajo (Diné) tribes, who are now linked by the uranium trucking routes passing through their lands. The Havasupai and Ute Mountain Ute tribes share concerns that toxic wastewater from uranium mining and milling may move through the ground and poison drinking water for future generations.

toggle caption Melissa Bailey/KFF Health News

A history of distrust

One spring morning in White Mesa, Yolanda Badback gazed out an open door not far from the highway and watched three uranium trucks drive by.

"There goes another one," Badback said with a tone of exhaustion. She is a Ute Mountain Ute member and leader of the White Mesa Concerned Community advocacy group that has been fighting the mill.

The mill receives 10 to 15 trucks each weekday, said Curtis Moore, senior vice president of marketing and corporate development at Energy Fuels, which has owned the facility since 2012. The majority pass through White Mesa.

The mill's business is picking up after a quiet 15 years, Moore said. The White Mesa Mill produced 1 million pounds of yellowcake last year; the company plans to more than double that this year, he said. The mill has also diversified into processing radioactive waste from as far away as Estonia and Japan, and received a $725 million conditional loan commitment from the Defense Department to scale up its domestic processing of rare earth elements.

Sponsor Message

The new rare earths business alone could create 100 permanent jobs, Moore said. About half of the mill's 105 workers are Indigenous; Moore estimated that no more than two belong to the Ute Mountain Ute Tribe.

"When it comes to tribes in the area, I do very much understand their skepticism of uranium," Moore said. "They've been lied to before."

A uranium boom driven by the U.S. government from the 1940s through the 1980s, much of it concentrated around the Four Corners area of Arizona, New Mexico, Utah and Colorado, exposed miners to heightened rates of mortality from lung and other cancers. Federal reviews found that the miners, many of them Navajo (Diné), were not warned about radiation risks even after government scientists understood the dangers. Mining companies left behind thousands of abandoned waste sites that have leached contamination into surrounding soil and water, including over 500 spots on and near the Navajo Nation.

But Moore said things have changed a lot since the 1950s. He said workers today are exposed to 15% to 20% of allowable radiation limits, and outside the mill it's "effectively zero."

Government agencies and Energy Fuels officials have said there's no evidence that the mill is affecting White Mesa's drinking water supply, which comes from a deep aquifer protected by a thick rock barrier known as an aquitard.

"It really is the perfect site for a uranium mill," Moore said.

Scott Clow, environmental programs director of the Ute Mountain Ute Tribe, said that deep aquifer does have quality issues — including arsenic, iron, and manganese — but the public drinking water is filtered and safe to drink.

Adam Wingate, uranium recovery manager at the Utah Department of Environmental Quality, said he understands why some residents are concerned. White Mesa is downslope in terms of underground water flow from the uranium mill.

Sponsor Message

If locals hear about the plume of contamination in a different, shallower aquifer beneath the mill — even if it's not the source of their drinking water — and their own water tastes funny, "that's a scary spot to be in," he said. But based on available evidence, Wingate said, locals' "health is not at risk because of the mill."

Even so, Lehi and Badback said that the tap water smells of sulfur and has a milky color, and that people in White Mesa typically don't drink it.

"I don't trust it," said Badback, whose family has been fighting the mill for decades. "My main goal is to shut the mill down."

An annual spiritual walk and protest sponsored by Badback's group has grown over the past decade amid deep distrust rooted in uranium mining's history. Much of the opposition centers on the mill's toxic waste, which is stored in five lined pits called tailings cells occupying 284 acres of land.

Badback vows to fight expansion plans that include new tailings cells located about a quarter-mile closer to the White Mesa community than the current ones. Moore said the cells will be triple-lined per modern standards.

"They want to expand south towards my reservation," Badback said. "That's the reason why I am standing up and doing whatever I can to stop that from happening."

Concerns about air quality

At a No Kings rally in March in Moab, about 80 miles north of White Mesa, Badback gave a speech and staffed a table offering T-shirts and information.

toggle caption Melissa Bailey/KFF Health News

"No Uranium," the T-shirts read. "Protect White Mesa Ute Community."

In 2021, her tribe passed a resolution stating that the White Mesa Mill "has had severe health impacts on the residents of White Mesa and should cease entirely."

While their psychological stress is palpable, other health effects have been hard to prove.

A 2023 federal health assessment concluded that radiation levels measured at the tribe's air monitor in the center of White Mesa between 2013 and 2019 were unlikely to harm human health. But the authors said they could not evaluate whether the mill's radon emissions could affect bordering properties or residents. They recommended that the tribe collect air samples closer to the mill, during times of heightened mill activity.

Sponsor Message

In December 2021, the Environmental Protection Agency found the mill was violating the Clean Air Act by failing to cover one of its tailings cells with liquid to limit emissions of radon, a known cause of lung cancer. The EPA called the violation "egregious in nature and duration" and temporarily barred the mill from receiving waste from Superfund cleanup sites.

The mill corrected the problem, according to state regulators, and passed its latest air quality review in 2025.

Still, some White Mesa residents remain uneasy. Badback and Lehi complained of odors, which they attribute to the mill, that smell like chemicals or rotten eggs. She has raised concerns about air quality and rates of cancer and asthma, which are being explored by a University of Utah health survey.

Moore denied that any odors from the mill could be smelled beyond the mill parking lot.

Utah air quality officials said the state does not conduct ambient air monitoring in White Mesa and does not regulate odors.

Watching the water

That spring day, Lehi continued to look for Entrance Spring. On the horizon lay the silhouette of Sleeping Ute Mountain, a landmark of the Ute Mountain Ute Tribe, said to be the body of a great warrior god.

Along the way, Lehi pointed out a circle of stones that he thought looked like an ancestral burial site. After parking the Jeep, he walked down a faint trail through a lush grove of willows and found his way into a streambed that he reckoned would lead to the spring.

The tribe doesn't rely on the spring for drinking water. But it's one of the seeps and springs that the tribe, the state and the company monitor, because they offer clues to whether the mill's waste ponds are leaking into a less protected aquifer.

In the late 2000s, an EPA report found elevated contamination by radionuclides — atoms that emit radiation as they decay — at Entrance Spring. EPA water samples found that uranium concentrations at times exceeded the federal drinking water standard. EPA and U.S. Geological Survey fieldwork suggested the uranium at Entrance Spring came not from leaking waste ponds but from dust that blew off the mill's ore storage pads.

Sponsor Message

The latest tests from 2025 showed Entrance Spring had uranium levels at 22.5 micrograms per liter (µg/L) — within the federal drinking standard of 30 µg/L but still elevated.

Clow said the tribe continues to keep a close eye on the seeps and springs.

"We're concerned about the pollution of those springs," he said. "We are looking towards many generations in the future here."

Clow is also closely watching the Burro Canyon Aquifer, which lies beneath the mill's toxic waste cells and feeds the local springs. A plume of chloroform and another of nitrates already pollute the aquifer, said Wingate, with the state. He said Energy Fuels is pumping out the contamination.

When contaminants increase, it's hard to prove whether they stemmed from natural causes or mill activity, since substances such as sulfate and manganese occur naturally in the local bedrock. So Clow, the company and state officials continually debate whether the tailings ponds are leaking.

What's not in dispute is that the mill produces radioactive waste — and once that exists, it can linger for tens of thousands of years.

Lehi followed the stream to where it ends in a curved grotto — the site of Entrance Spring. Water oozed from a rock face into a pool, offering cool relief from the desert. Lehi looked around with wonder at the dripping green moss. A descendant of medicine men, Lehi said he feels a duty to protect the landscape as his ancestors did, even if the tribe doesn't currently use this spring for drinking water.

"Water is life," Lehi said, "because that's where we all began."

This article was supported by The Water Desk, an independent journalism initiative based at the University of Colorado-Boulder's Center for Environmental Journalism.

KFF Health News is a national newsroom that produces in-depth journalism about health issues and is one of the core operating programs at KFF — the independent source for health policy research, polling, and journalism.

World.title: How a road could change West Africa's urban future
World.content:
It propelled the women who dominated the market into new wealth. They became an example of how working-class enterprise could lead to genuine prosperity.

They were known by the luxury cars they bought, like Mercedes-Benz, and were memorialized in popular culture as glamorous, wealthy figures, riding their cars through the capital.

Bundles of colorful fabrics fill dozens of boutiques at the sprawling Grand MarchÃ© in LomÃ© â including the Dutch wax fabrics dense with swirling, floral designs, which are at the heart of the Nana Benzâs fairy-tale rise.

Emmanuel Akinwotu/NPR

On the walls of dozens of textile boutiques, many of which are franchises of the Dutch company Vlisco, are pictures of the women who founded them. In one store, set up by Marguerite Sewoa-Lawson, the upper floor of her boutique becomes an archival exhibition, the walls lined with framed photographs telling a success story beloved across the region.

But to many, their achievements now feel out of reach. The Nana Benz inspired thousands of women to join the trade, which saturated the market.

Economic shocks in the region also affected the market, according to experts, including the devaluation of the regional currency in 1994 and the initially turbulent impact of reforms backed by the International Monetary Fund. The reforms promoted more liberal trade, with few protections for local industries.

According to widespread analysis of the reforms, they diminished the dominance of Dutch wax fabrics and led to the rise of cheaper Chinese imports that have further devalued the market.

World.title: Spain confronts influx of solar eclipse tourists while still battling wildfires
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Hundreds of thousands of tourists have descended on Spain in the hopes of experiencing Wednesday's solar eclipse.

But the celestial event comes amid elevated temperatures and an increased risk of wildfires in Spain, raising alarm bells for authorities hoping to ensure the boom in astrotourism doesn’t come with lasting fire damage.

"We've had an extremely tough summer in Spain, with yet another series of major forest fires. That's why we must restrict any kind of activity that could generate a spark," Virginia Barcones, secretary general for civil ​protection and emergencies at Spain's Interior Ministry, told Reuters.

A heat wave has been smothering much of Europe since May, and Spain is currently grappling with a devastating wildfire season. More than 603,000 acres (2,440 square kilometres) of land have been burned in around 400 fires so far this year, according to the European Forest ​Fire Information System.

To ensure that eclipse tourists don’t add to this number, authorities are deploying 35,000 officers on Wednesday to large, outdoor gatherings in the hopes of spotting and stopping any new fires that may start, according to Barcones.

Forest rangers work in a wildfire-scorched area near Casillas, Avila province, Spain on July 30. (AP Photo/Olmo Calvo)

Spain is one of the best viewing locations for Wednesday's solar eclipse — the narrow band of totality, around 200 kilometres across, also crosses northern Russia, eastern Greenland and western Iceland, clipping the northeastern tip of Portugal and curving across a wide swathe of northern Spain, ending at the Balearic Islands. Around 15 million people live in its path, mostly in Spain.

Only those in the path of totality will witness the moon fully covering the sun. In Canada, a partial eclipse will be visible, with those in Newfoundland seeing the most coverage. Authorities are reminding viewers to always use eclipse glasses to protect their eyes.

This will be the first time a full solar eclipse has been visible from mainland Spain in 120 years, and the excitement has sparked a flurry of travel.

A fishing boat is silhouetted during a partial solar eclipse in Halifax on March 29, 2025. (The Canadian Press/Darren Calabrese)

Earlier this summer, authorities in Spain announced that special measures approved by the Ministry of the Interior would be in place for the solar eclipse to handle the large crowds anticipated. Searches for lodging along the eclipse’s path of totality spiked as the event grew nearer, according to Expedia Group, with Valencia, Spain, seeing a 245 per cent increase in searches compared to the previous year.

A total of 660 official viewing sites have been outlined by regional governments in the hopes of handling the expected influx of more than 440,000 people. Authorities estimate around 1.5 million people could be on the road during the day to head to viewing sites. Both national and local authorities are warning tourists against using barbecues or going into dry countryside where fire risk is higher.

Are you currently in or travelling to Europe to watch the solar eclipse? We want to hear from you. Send us your photos or videos and share your experience at ask@cbc.ca.

The eclipse is anticipated to contribute more than 347 million euros to Spain's economy, according to a July economic impact study by the Ministry of Economy, Trade and Business.

Dry conditions, fire fears

Three major wildfires are still burning in the provinces of Huelva, Segovia and Huesca. Only one of the severe blazes is in the path of totality, according to Joe McNorton, a scientist with the European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts: the Las Peñas de Riglos wildfire active to the north of Zaragoza, which "could pose a danger if astro-tourists venture into the area."

Burnt trees stand in an area scorched by a wildfire near Vila Vella, Valencia province, Spain, on July 30. (Damian Torres/The Associated Press)

But the forest fire index across much of the Iberian Peninsula and the Balearic Islands is expected to reach "very high or extreme levels" on the day of the eclipse, according to AEMET , Spain's meteorological agency. And the country is perilously dry: last month, only 4.3 millimetres of rainfall was recorded across mainland Spain, a quarter of the normal precipitation expected this time of year. It was the driest July on record, according to AEMET.

"Around 90 per cent of wildfires are human-caused, so the presence of many more people in rural areas inevitably brings more potential ignition sources," McNorton told CBC News.

WATCH | Heat wave in Europe threatens to fuel further wildfires: Heat wave threatens to further fuel Europe’s wildfires | Duration 2:02 Wildfires in France have forced 4,000 more people along the Atlantic coast to evacuate as another heat wave threatens to fuel the flames there and in neighbouring Spain.

AEMET is forecasting temperatures upwards of 35 C on eclipse day, with some regions reaching 40 C, although peak temperatures will be down two to five degrees by the time of the eclipse.

Reykjavík, Iceland, will see totality at 5:48 p.m. local time, but viewers in Spain won’t see the eclipse enter totality until just before sunset, with northwestern Spain entering totality starting at around 8:28 p.m. local time. At its maximum, totality will last two minutes and 18 seconds, although this will vary by location.

Eclipse fervor holding

Even amid a heat wave and wildfires, eclipse travelers have not been deterred. Jan Cami, a professor in the physics and astronomy department at the University of Western Ontario in London, Ont., says he is unsurprised.

"It’s an event where you don't need to be a scientist at all to actually enjoy that this is an absolute spectacle that nature has provided for us," Cami told CBC News.

During maximum totality, the temperature drops, and stars and planets become briefly visible during the day, an experience so "overwhelming" that those who witness it often start making plans for their next trip to see it again, he said. He has colleagues both in Spain and on a cruise in Iceland waiting for their chance to see the sun vanish on Wednesday.

A view of totality during the solar eclipse on April 8, 2024, in Hot Springs National Park, Ark. (Nick Ingram/The Associated Press)

"I think [travelling for celestial events] is a great opportunity at the same time to learn about other parts of the world."

It’s this sense of shared meaning that Cami is hoping will touch tourists in Spain – that those who battle the heat to see the eclipse will reflect on the struggles of the country they’re in, and how far-reaching the impacts of climate change are.

Maarten Savelkoel, 76, from the Netherlands, visits a campsite to see the total solar eclipse, in Arija, Spain, on Tuesday. (Borja Suarez/Reuters)

The 2026 eclipse is just the first in a trio of solar eclipses in the next few years that will be visible from Spain. Two more are expected, on Aug. 2, 2027, and Jan. 26, 2028, respectively.

The 2027 solar eclipse could prompt even more astrotourism, Cami predicts. The path of totality will cross southern Spain before continuing to Morocco, Algeria, Tunisia, Libya, Egypt, Saudi Arabia and Yemen.

"You can see the total eclipse of next year while [at] the pyramids of Giza," he said.

World.title: Manitoba mother whose 'little angel' died in CFS care says she was trying to get kids back
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

A grieving mother says someone needs to be held accountable after her four-year-old daughter died in the care of Child and Family Services and her two other children were taken to a Winnipeg hospital with serious injuries.

Manitoba First Nations Police Service officers were called to a home in Long Plain First Nation on Sunday morning after the four-year-old was found by first responders with injuries and in medical distress, RCMP said in a news release Tuesday.

The girl was pronounced dead and her two sisters, a one-year-old and two-year-old, were taken to the hospital — one of them in critical condition.

Her mother said her four-year-old daughter was starting kindergarten in September and was about to celebrate her fifth birthday later this month.

"She was just a little angel. She loved her little siblings." the mom told CBC Tuesday. "She loved to sing, she loved to dance."

CBC is not identifying the mother to protect the identity of the two children who remain in the care of Child and Family Services.

RCMP Major Crimes Services said they took over the investigation from First Nations police due to the nature of the girl's death and the injuries to the siblings. No charges have been laid.

Children under care of CFS

The children were under the care of Waywayseecapo CFS, a western Manitoba agency based in Waywayseecapo First Nation, according to emails viewed by CBC.

A representative from Waywayseecapo CFS agency — which is under the umbrella of the Southern First Nations Network of Care authority — said the agency is not commenting on the death at this time.

The mom spent the last two days visiting her children at Health Sciences Centre's children's hospital.

"They're just babies and they're just sweethearts," said the girls' mother, who spoke to CBC Tuesday outside of the hospital.

The mother said her kids had been in care since October and the last time she saw them was in February.

At that time, she says they looked skinny and she could see bruising on one child's eyes — a concern she raised with her CFS worker.

"I had a gut feeling something was happening and nobody listened to me," she said.

Families minister to do internal investigation

Manitoba's Families Minister Nahanni Fontaine said her department will be doing its own internal investigation and they have reported the death to the Manitoba Advocate for Children and Youth to also investigate.

In an emailed statement, Fontaine said she is "deeply saddened by the tragic death of this young child."

She cannot comment further on the circumstances of the case due to the active RCMP investigation, she said.

Families Minister Nahanni Fontaine said the province will conduct its own internal investigation into the death. (Tyson Koschik/CBC)

Her government remains committed to "working with the Southern Network of Care and all authorities to strengthen supports and ensure children and families receive the care and services they need," she said in the statement.

A spokesperson for the Southern Chiefs' Organization, which represents 33 First Nations in southern Manitoba including Waywayseecappo First Nation, sent condolences to the family.

"Given the ongoing investigations into the circumstances surrounding the child’s death and the injuries sustained by the other children, SCO will not comment further or speculate at this time," the spokesperson said in an emailed statement.

'Time to take my baby back in a casket'

After her kids were apprehended in October, the mom says she went into a four-week treatment program in December, took parenting classes and was hoping to get her kids back this summer.

"I did everything, I went to treatment, I did the programs, I stayed sober. I cleaned my house," she said.

"Then just nothing was done about it. And now look, time to take my baby back in a casket and my other girls are just so broken."

She is speaking about what happened to her daughter because she doesn't want to see another death in care and she wants answers as to how this happened.

"I just want her voice to be heard and make sure it doesn't happen to any other kids. Some things need to be done about this," she said.

"All I wanted was them to be home with me where they were safe. And nobody listened."

World.title: What to know about the trial of Lindsay Clancy, woman accused of killing her 3 children
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

WARNING: This article contains details about violence against children and attempted suicide:

The Lindsay Clancy murder trial is making headlines around the world as jurors hear harrowing details of the Massachusetts mother who killed her three young children.

Clancy's legal team does not deny that she killed her children, but is arguing she shouldn't be held criminally responsible because she was mentally ill — in the grip of bipolar disorder and postpartum psychosis, a rare condition that the Centre for Addiction and Mental Health says occurs in approximately one to two cases per 1,000 births. Postpartum psychosis can cause extreme mood swings, delusions and confusion, according to the Society of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists of Canada.

Prosecutors argue Clancy is guilty of three counts of first-degree murder, having plotted to get her husband out of the house so she could carry out the murders.

The trial, which is being held in Plymouth, Mass., is being livestreamed on CourtTV and major Boston TV stations, as well as YouTube. On Tuesday, the trial moved into day 11, and proceedings are expected to continue for several more weeks.

Here are some details about the case and what court has heard.

The killings

Clancy, a former labour and delivery nurse, was struggling with her mental health and seeing multiple specialists in 2022. The court has heard she was prescribed 13 different psychiatric medications across different providers.

Her attorneys say Clancy did everything she could to seek help: She turned to multiple outpatient providers, tried various drugs they prescribed, called a suicide hotline, went to an emergency room and approached but wasn’t accepted into a hospital-based, full-day treatment program for women with postpregnancy mental health problems. Clancy also checked herself into a psychiatric hospital for several days.

Rather than improving her condition, her attorneys and family say the shifting cocktail of psychiatric medications made things worse.

Cellphone records show that on Jan. 24, 2023, she texted her husband Patrick late in the afternoon, asking him to pick up takeout and medicine.

During his absence from their Duxbury, Mass., home, prosecutors say Clancy used exercise bands to strangle their three children: five-year-old Cora, three-year-old Dawson and eight-month-old Callan. She then cut her own wrists and throat and jumped out of a second-storey window in an apparent suicide attempt.

Clancy, who turned 36 on Tuesday, was paralyzed from the waist down and has been attending the court proceedings in a wheelchair.

Court hears diary entries

Opening statements began on July 27, after an 18-member jury was selected.

Patrick Clancy, Lindsay's now former husband, took the stand early, detailing her mental health struggles and his experience on the day of the killings. Jurors were shaken when his 911 call was played in court.

The court later heard from Duxbury first responders, crime scene analysts and the family's nanny, who said Lindsay was a "wonderful mom who loved her kids."

Clancy's diary entries were also read in court, including a section where she wrote that she was “completely overwhelmed” trying to take care of her children.

“I feel like I’m drowning every day,” she wrote.

She sobbed in court when details of the autopsy reports were read.

Testimony from psychiatrists

Recent days have focused on Clancy's mental state, including testimonies from her psychiatrists and mental health experts.

On Monday her lawyer probed Dr. Jennifer Tufts, who saw Clancy via video meetings from September 2022 until the day before the killings.

Defence lawyer Kevin Reddington questioned Tufts' expertise, prescribing decisions and overall treatment, spotlighting her use of 25-minute video appointments and the series of recommended pharmaceuticals.

Defence attorney Kevin Reddington, left, questions psychiatrist Dr. Jennifer Tufts about her hand written notes on Monday. (Greg Derr/Pool/The Patriot Ledger)

"I do not believe that I've been negligent," Tufts testified.

Clancy is suing Tufts and other practitioners in civil court.

On Tuesday, another of Clancy's psychiatrists, Rebecca Jollotta, testified about a concerning mid-December call with the couple during which she heard Clancy had her "worst day" and was "having persistent, intrusive thoughts of suicide."

Prosecutor Shanan Buckingham has urged jurors not to view the trial as "a public debate about women's mental health and how the medical system treats women," but rather to focus on the specific actions Clancy took and the intent behind them.

If convicted of murder, Clancy faces life in prison without parole.

If found not guilty due to a lack of criminal responsibility, she would be committed to a state mental health facility.

Legal expert Margaret McLean told Parade that Clancy's case would then shift to a "civil commitment process" overseen by the court and mental health experts.

Clancy could eventually be released under strict conditions, or, if her illness is deemed "chronic and dangerous," she could remain institutionalized for the rest of her life.

World.title: From last place to the post-season? Here's how the 2026 Blue Jays could pull it off
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results. It's been a frustrating season for the Toronto Blue Jays after the team made it all the way to Game 7 of the World Series last year, but a winning surge in the past two weeks has kept their playoff hopes alive. The CBC's Greg Ross has more on the Jays' turnaround and their chances of making it to the post-season. Prime Minister Mark Carney says "you've got to believe" the Toronto Blue Jays can still make the playoffs. But can they, really? The Jays have played some scrappy baseball lately, as the team finds itself on the fringes of playoff contention with a quarter of the season to go and it's still possible they might find a way to the post-season in the anemic American League. Toronto beat the Boston Red Sox tonight, in a 5-3 victory that improved their season record to 58-63 and kept the team in the hunt for a potential playoff spot. Thanks for the sweater, Karla.

My message to Jays Nation: you've got to believe. pic.twitter.com/oP6IQ9dHmJ —MarkJCarney "At this point, you just kind of throw everything other than winning out the window and show up every day and try to win," Jays infielder and all-star Ernie Clement told CBC News, earlier Tuesday. There are a half-dozen teams, including Toronto, that are within four games of the last wild-card spot in the wider American League — and the Blue Jays would have to leap past all of them to secure a return to the post-season. Here's a look at why the Jays are where they are with just over 40 games to go, and what they have to do to get back to the post-season. From the World Series to last place? That's the reality: Toronto has gone from a team that competed for a World Series title last fall to a team curently sitting in last place in the American Leage East. They can't win the division at this point, so that means they'll have to claim a wild-card spot to reach the post-season. WATCH | The end of an era for some Toronto fan favourites: Blue Jays lose fan favourites in big trades | Duration 2:09 Less than a year after competing for the MLB championship, the Toronto Blue Jays made some big trades ahead of the deadline, including fan favourites Daulton Varsho and pitcher Kevin Gausman. The win over Boston Tuesday night improved Toronto's season record to 58-63 — 12 fewer wins than they had at the same point last year. At present, the Tampa Bay Rays lead the AL East, followed by the New York Yankees in second place, and the resurgent Boston Red Sox — who put together lengthy win streaks in July and August — in third. The Baltimore Orioles (with a 58-62 record) and the Jays sit in fourth and fifth place. Just 2 teams have done it According to Elias Sports Bureau, the official statistician of Major League Baseball (MLB), there are just two teams that have stood at 58-63 through 121 games — the same record the Jays have right now — that went on to make the playoffs in the wild-card era: The 2024 Detroit Tigers and the 2009 Minnesota Twins. Randy Robles of Elias Sports Bureau believes "there's some hope" for the Jays, noting that if there ever was a year for a struggling team to still have a chance, it would be this one, when so many American League teams have been playing so poorly. Blue Jays rookie Charles McAdoo runs the bases at Toronto's Rogers Centre after hitting a solo home run in Monday's game against the Boston Red Sox. (Getty Images) What it will take Toronto has begun to claw its way to a better record, claiming series wins against the Washington Nationals, the St. Louis Cardinals, the Houston Astros and the Philadelphia Phillies in the past couple of weeks. That winning trend has to continue for the team to have a shot at the post-season: "They gotta get to .500," Robles told CBC News, referring to the point when a team has won as many games as it has lost. The Texas Rangers, the team currently sitting in the third wild-card spot the Jays are vying for, was only one game above the .500 mark prior to Tuesday's matchups. All the teams seeking to take the Rangers' spot — Toronto included — currently have losing records. Summing up the challenge the Blue Jays face in climbing the standings, Toronto Star baseball columnist Mike Wilner saw a certain parity in the teams involved in the wild-card fight. "Every team in front of the Blue Jays kind of stinks," Wilner told CBC News. "The problem is, the Blue Jays kind of stink, too." Dylan Cease is the ace of the Blue Jays' starting pitching staff and in the hunt for a Cy Young Award this season. (Paul Beaty/The Associated Press) Cease leads the rotation The Jays are thin on starting pitching right now, but the rotation includes pitching ace Dylan Cease, the newly acquired José Soriano, Shane Bieber, as well as veteran Max Scherzer. Cease is on the hunt for a Cy Young Award, and has been in the midst of a sizzling run this summer that included bid for a no-hitter in July that he carried into the ninth inning. He started Tuesday's game against Boston, going five innings and striking out seven. Soriano was solid in his recent Blue Jays debut. Bieber, who missed most of the first half of the season, has been battling for consistency since rejoining the team in June. Scherzer has had two decent starts for Toronto this month — and the team will be counting on him to deliver more if they have a shot at a wild card. "We have a job to do: Every time we come to the park, we've got to win," Scherzer told CBC News. In the bullpen, the Jays will continue to look to closer Louis Varland and workhorse reliever Tyler Rogers in high-leverage situations. Rookie pitcher Spencer Miles, as well as relievers Braydon Fisher and Mason Fluharty will also be key to any push for the post-season. Kazuma Okamoto rounds the bases after a July 28 home run at Nationals Park. The rookie is leading the Jays in home runs this year with 24. (Brad Mills/Imagn Images/Reuters) What about the bats? Hitting has been a real problem for the Blue Jays this year. The team sits near the bottom of the major leagues in terms of home runs, runs scored and on-base percentage. Only two Blue Jays have a double-digit home run total: Kazuma Okamoto (24) and Springer (12). Last year, Toronto had four players who swatted 20-plus homers. This year, they'll be fortunate to have two.

World.title: What’s Quebec identity anyway? These Quebecers had a lot to say
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

There are two words that always seem to come up in political discourse in this province: Quebec identity or, in French, l’identité Québécoise.

But what does it mean ? Who defines it? Ahead of the Oct. 5 provincial election, I asked a cross section of Quebecers — and they offered a wealth of perspectives.

What follows is a series of those candid and nuanced conversations. I chatted with two women who left India and Pakistan in the 1970s for Quebec under René Lévesque. I met young sovereignists with Indigenous and Maghrebi roots, respectively.

I also caught up with one woman who identifies as a Montrealer — not a Quebecer — and two others who told me how they juggle their Quebec pride while fervently defending their English-language institutions.

Here's what they had to say.

A more ‘inclusive,’ welcoming Quebec

What does Quebec identity mean to these women with South Asian roots? | Duration 7:00 What does Quebec identity mean to Dolores Chew and Shaheen Ashraf? The two women immigrated to Quebec in the mid-1970s and one of them voted ‘Yes’ in the 1980 referendum.

Quebec has been home to Dolores Chew and Shaheen Ashraf for more than 50 years. And they still enjoy South Asian comforts like a cup of chai.

Over tea and snacks, they fondly recall a Quebec under René Lévesque. One of them voted ‘Yes’ in the 1980 referendum. But their sense of belonging changed after that.

The youth behind Quebec's sovereignty movement

2 sovereignists — with Moroccan and Indigenous roots — explain why Quebec should be a country | Duration 7:56 Nabil Ben Ali Ouriaghli and Benjamin Gingras say they identify with an independent Quebec that doesn’t assimilate anybody. But some values commonly promoted in Quebec, they say, are still up for debate.

Nabil Ben Ali Ouriaghli and Benjamin Gingras are both members of Oui Quebec, a citizen-led movement promoting sovereignty. They say their vision of an independent Quebec is one that focuses on inclusion and what brings people together.

Have a story about what Quebec identity means to you? Reach out to Sudha Krishnan at sudha.krishnan@cbc.ca

But they recognize there’s work to do in getting that message out.

A proud Montrealer — not Quebecer or Canadian

Why this Montrealer’s identity is rooted in the city – and not in Quebec and Canada | Duration 7:41 While Shereen Joseph proudly identifies as a Malaysian Montrealer, she says her identity is less tied to Quebec and Canada and wonders if she would feel as welcome if she left the city.

Western Canada didn’t quite feel like home, but Montreal sure did.

When Shereen Joseph moved to the Plateau-Mont-Royal borough, she found the identity that truly resonated with her: Montrealer. She explains how her Malaysian roots helped her embrace the city and the French language — and why the language tensions in this province seem so foreign.

Fighting for English-language institutions

What Quebec identity means to these 2 bilingual English school board commissioners | Duration 7:48 Allison Saunders claims her bilingual Quebec identity by living in both worlds — whether that means watching French TV or representing English education. As a young university student raised in the predominantly French-speaking neighbourhood of Rivière-des-Prairies, Susan Perera emphasizes the importance of bilingualism. But they both worry about young English-speaking students who are questioning their future in Quebec.

For Susan Perera and Allison Saunders, English-language schools are not just about education, they’re also about community and promoting a bilingual Quebec.

Both English school board commissioners proudly claim their Quebec identity. But at times, Saunders feels she "does not tick all the boxes" when it comes to how some people define what it means to be a Quebecer.

World.title: 'An absolute gut punch': Dozens facing unemployment as an Ottawa Metro converts to Food Basics
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

A Metro grocery store in Ottawa's South Keys neighbourhood will be replaced by a Food Basics this fall, costing dozens of employees their jobs.

Metro Inc. says the store, which closed Wednesday, is being converted to a Food Basics to better meet customer needs in the area.

"We regularly assess our store network based on a range of factors, including local market conditions and store performance," a spokesperson with the company wrote in a statement to CBC. "Moving to a discount banner reflects the type of market and demand in the area."

The decision still came as a shock to employees at Metro's Southgate location, however.

"We were all just stunned," said Justin Braganza, a meat cutter who has worked at the store for more than 30 years.

Braganza, who's also a volunteer steward with the United Food and Commercial Workers union, said he and his colleagues were informed of the impending closure in May by their regional manager and another Metro representative who cited financial pressure.

"They said that rent had gone up and that they didn’t feel that our store was profitable enough to sustain the Metro model," he explained. "We were told very bluntly that we were all being terminated."

CBC asked Metro if the cost of rent contributed to its decision to convert the Southgate store, but the company maintained the change was made based on local market conditions and customer needs.

The Southgate Metro employed 72 people. Metro told CBC that under to the terms of their collective agreement, those workers don't have the option to transfer to other Metro stores.

"Employees who are interested in working at the new Food Basics store are invited to apply and will be considered through that process," the company wrote.

Employees blindsided

The collective agreement for the new Food Basics store requires Metro to hire a minimum of 10 part-time and five full-time employees who worked at the Southgate Metro and who apply to work at the new store, a spokesperson with the company explained.

Because Metro and Food Basics operate under different wage structures, if a former Metro Southgate employee is hired at the new store their seniority will be taken into consideration within the Food Basics pay band, the spokesperson said.

That's little comfort to employees like Braganza, however.

"It was just an absolute gut punch," he said. "They don’t use meat cutters at Food Basics, so I don't have a job waiting for me at this new store if I was even successful in the application process."

He said some of his colleagues could have even more at stake.

"One or two of our employees are even here on work permits, and them remaining in Canada depends on them having a job, and to not have a job, that really makes their situation so much more tenuous."

Some Metro customers were also disappointed at the news.

"To me, it's just disrespect for the workers. That's what bothers me very deeply," said Michael Vorobej. "I think Metro just wants to up their profit margin, and they want to do it on the backs of the people that have been working for them for so long."

The United Food and Commercial Workers union told CBC that representatives from locals 175 and 633 negotiated 'enhanced options' for its members including severance benefits and job opportunities at the new Food Basics store. (Dalson Chen/CBC)

Union negotiated 'enhanced options' for workers

The union representing workers at the Southgate Metro declined an interview, but in a statement to CBC said its representatives had reached out to Metro to advocate for its members' rights.

"As a result, UFCW Locals 175 and 633 negotiated enhanced options for our members at the Metro store, including job opportunities at the new Food Basics store and enhanced severance options," the union wrote.

It also said it held individual meetings with affected members to outline those options, "which was well received and appreciated by the employees."

A lawyer who specializes in employment and labour law reviewed the collective agreement between Metro Inc. and UFCW Local 175, and told CBC the deal does allow the company to lay employees off due to a shortage of work.

"That leaves the question ... if Metro is basically shutting down and then opening up and rebranding itself as a Food Basics, is there actually a shortage of work? Did they actually not have enough work for these positions, or is it more a change of corporate identity?” asked Nelligan Law partner Malini Vijaykumar.

Vijaykumar said a union may file a grievance challenging a company's claim of a work shortage. It may also argue that a company's actions constitute anti-union behaviour, opening the door to litigation.

"That can take months and months, and all the while your employees are out of work and out of pay," she said.

Malini Vijaykumar is a partner with Nelligan Law who specializes in employment and labour law. (Nelligan Law)

Alternatively, these cases can be resolved through settlements between the union and the employer. Vijaykumar explained that these deals often include confidentiality clauses and bar unions from filing grievances.

"Unions are typically pretty vocal," Vijaykumar said. "Where you're not seeing that and where an enhanced severance arrangement and job opportunities and that kind of thing seem to have been worked out, it may be a sign that there has been a sort of agreement worked out between the parties."

If that has happened, both sides will be cautious about communicating details of any deal, she said.

Meanwhile, Braganza said he and other employees are feeling sidelined and without much recourse.

"It illustrates that workers have very few rights in this situation," he said. "The employer holds all the cards."

Braganza said he's been reflecting on the relationships he’s built with colleagues and customers that he'll have to leave behind.

"It's like we were a little family, and now with this closure we're all going to go our separate ways and it’s going to be hard," he said.

World.title: Trump says Secret Service wanted him on 'different plane' for NATO trip due to security concerns
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

U.S. President ​Donald Trump took a secret military flight from Turkey last month in an operation that involved him being moved between aircraft in a catering truck, a deception prompted by an Iranian assassination threat.

The White House said at the time that the president was flying aboard Air Force One from Turkey, where he had attended a NATO summit, to Britain. But moments ‌after Trump boarded the plane, he left it in secret via the catering truck and boarded another aircraft for the flight to Britain, the Washington Post said on Monday, quoting unnamed sources.

Trump confirmed the events on Tuesday, saying the Secret Service and military wanted him on a "different plane" due to a threat that he insisted didn't scare him.

He also downplayed the risk to the people he left on the plan, including White House officials, security and support staff, and reporters.

"They wanted me to go on a different flight, different plane," Trump told reporters after returning from an event in Ohio, saying he had little choice in the matter.

"I guess there was a threat out there. I didn't really ask too much about it," he said. "I get a lot of threats."

WATCH | Trump switched planes because of security threat: Trump secretly swaps planes by hiding in a catering truck: reports | Duration 2:01 U.S. President Donald Trump secretly swapped planes by hiding in a catering truck when leaving the NATO summit in Turkey last month, according to U.S. media reports. The move was allegedly due to security concerns after threats from Iran.

Plane change prompts security questions

Trump had taken a newly renovated Qatari-donated jet to Ankara for the NATO summit but unexpectedly announced he would use an older Air Force One when ​departing the country, a move that prompted questions about the newer plane's security.

The trip to ​NATO was the first international travel for the new plane, whose speedy upgrades triggered questions over its cost and security, and took place as hostilities escalated with Iran, which borders Turkey.

Before departing Ankara, Trump said on his social media site Truth Social that he would use ​an older baby blue Air Force One plane "for old time's sake" to RAF Mildenhall in Britain while the new ⁠plane stopped at the same base so ⁠U.S. service members stationed there could tour the aircraft.

Journalists who thought they were travelling with Trump on the older Air Force One, which was effectively used as a decoy, reported being advised to keep their window shades in the press cabin closed.

The ‌Post said aside from reporters, some White House staff also believed that the president was on board.

When asked later by reporters why they had to keep their shades shut during the flight, Trump said it was because they were "probably on a dangerous flight."

He went on to say: “But if I go, you go. Right?"
