World.title: Merz’s deal with the Taliban alarms Afghan dissidents in Germany
World.content:
Under pressure from the rising far right, Berlin is letting Taliban officials staff Afghan missions in exchange for more deportations. Activists say the arrangement puts them at risk.

Zarmina Paryani and her four sisters fear they may soon have to again face the persecutors they fled from in Afghanistan — and this time inside Germany.

Paryani and her sisters were imprisoned twice in Kabul for protesting against the Taliban after the Afghan militants retook the capital in 2021, the 27-year-old said. After going into hiding for several months, the family eventually made their way to Germany in search of safe haven.

But now, Berlin has struck a Faustian bargain that allows the Taliban to deepen its diplomatic foothold in Germany in return for cooperation on deporting Afghan migrants back to Afghanistan. For Paryani and other Afghan activists who resisted the Taliban at home, the arrangement is giving their former persecutors new leverage over their lives in exile.





“It’s hard to accept that my fate and my affairs are being discussed with the very same representatives whose oppression, prisons, whippings and violence I fled from,” Paryani, who worked as a midwife in Kabul and now lives in western Germany, told POLITICO.

German Chancellor Friedrich Merz’s government first struck a deal with the Afghan government announced last October that gives Taliban officials control of diplomatic missions in Berlin and Bonn in exchange for permission to return Afghan migrants directly to Afghanistan. That cooperation was deepened early this summer with a deal that allows more Taliban officials to work in Germany in return for cooperation on additional deportation flights — now up to three per month.

Under the new deal, Germany has expanded deportations to include not only Afghan men convicted of crimes, but also, more broadly, Afghan men with no protected status or legal right to remain in Germany.

The agreement with the Taliban makes Germany an outlier in Europe, making it the first EU country to allow Taliban-appointed officials to work in diplomatic missions inside the country. Before the agreement, Western-oriented Afghan officials representing the former government in Afghanistan had remained in charge.

The arrangement comes as Merz’s government grapples with rock-bottom approval ratings and the rise of the anti-immigrant Alternative for Germany (AfD) party, now the country’s most popular political force, according to polls. The AfD’s surge comes ahead of two elections in the former East Germany, where the far-right party is ahead in polls by wide margins. In one of those states, Saxony-Anhalt, the party may take real governing power for the first time since it was founded in 2013, a result that would serve as a great humiliation for the conservative Merz, who was elected chancellor last year partly on a promise to crack down on migration.





The AfD’s rise is piling pressure on the chancellor to deliver on his election pledge to deport more migrants — even as he insists that working with the Taliban does not legitimize a regime notorious for its human rights abuses. Overall, Afghans are the third-largest group of refugees or people who have fled war to come to Germany, behind Ukrainians and Syrians.

“We are not extending a hand to this Taliban regime,” Merz said in the German parliament in June. “Rather, we are seeking cooperation at the necessary technical level, which is in our country’s national interest.”

‘Nightmares’ and ‘psychological distress’

For Afghan rights activists in Germany, one of the worst consequences of Berlin’s deal with the Taliban is that it may particularly put at risk some 35,000 Afghans who came to Germany under special humanitarian programs for people deemed especially vulnerable to the Taliban. They include Paryani and her sisters in addition to thousands of human rights activists and Afghans who worked with the German military during its nearly two-decade presence in the country.

Paryani and others fear they will have to face the Taliban when attempting to renew their Afghan passports — which they need to extend their humanitarian visas — at Afghan diplomatic missions. Another 321,000 Afghans live in Germany as refugees or with other forms of protected status. They do not necessarily need Afghan passports, unless they want to apply for a permanent residence status.

More generally, activists and refugees also fear the Taliban, with their growing presence in Germany, could gain access to personal information held in databases in German missions, including details about their families, making them susceptible to blackmail and extortion.

Afghan activists speak at a protest camp at Berlin’s Alexanderplatz on Aug. 15, 2025, the fourth anniversary of the Taliban takeover. | Sean Gallup/Getty Images

“Given my personal history and my stance on extremism, I am concerned for my safety and that of my family,” one former teacher from Afghanistan granted anonymity due to his fear of retribution from the Taliban told POLITICO.

The former teacher, who lives in Germany with a humanitarian visa, said German immigration officials have asked him to renew his expired Afghan passport, a request that he fears will force him to deal directly with his persecutors.

“This situation continues to cause me significant psychological distress,” he said. “Sometimes I wake up at night because of nightmares related to the Taliban and this situation.”

‘Vulnerable to blackmail’

With its handling of the Taliban, Merz’s government is setting a precedent that will be closely watched by other EU countries. Government officials in Austria and Belgium have said they’re watching Germany’s cooperation with the Taliban closely. Taliban officials also held talks focused on deportations with the EU Commission in June in Brussels.

But Hamid Nangialay Kabiri, the former head of the Afghan consulate in Bonn, who quit last September in protest over the initial deal allowing Taliban officials to serve in diplomatic missions in Germany, warned that the German government’s decision to cooperate with the Afghan regime would come back to haunt it — and that the Taliban would use their new leverage over Germany to advance their interests in Europe, including by building networks that intimidate dissidents.

“They are destroying my country, and now they are coming here,” he said. “They are not thinking of diplomacy. They have a lot of plans in their mind.”





It’s a sentiment politicians inside the left-leaning opposition also share.

“The German government has made itself vulnerable to blackmail,” Schahina Gambir, a lawmaker for the Greens who was born in Kabul, told POLITICO. “We’re seeing recognition through the back door. The Taliban are being granted access to embassies, they’re being granted immunity, they’re given channels for dialogue — and at the same time, the situation for women and girls in Afghanistan is getting worse and worse.”

There are already signs that the Taliban are exercising their newfound leverage.

Last May, Kabul unexpectedly halted a deportation flight at the last minute, seemingly seeking to extract additional concessions from the German government. A couple of weeks later, Berlin announced the terms of the latest agreement allowing additional Taliban-appointed officials to work at diplomatic missions in Germany.

Officials in Berlin depicted the new deal as a victory and a practical necessity, allowing for more deportations.





“To increase the number of repatriations, more passports must be issued, more identities must be verified, and so on,” Martin Giese, a spokesperson for Germany’s foreign ministry, said at the time. “To this end, it will also be necessary for more consular officials to be involved.”

But Paryani, the Afghan midwife who fled to Germany with her four sisters, said the Taliban would use their new power to torment them in the country they had sought safety in.

“A Taliban member once wrote to me: ‘Just wait until our embassy in Germany reopens. Then we’ll find you there,'” she said of a comment that had surfaced under one of her social media posts about two years ago. She then deemed it irrelevant because it seemed so unrealistic.

“Today, I feel as though that threat has become a reality,” she said.

World.title: Zelenskyy’s Balkan fumble
World.content:
Since Zelenskyy’s visit, Vučić threatened to physically redirect the Iber River that runs from Serbia to Kosovo in retaliation for Kosovo demolishing Serb-owned houses along the reservoir’s shore. Such a move would drain the reservoir supplying much of Kosovo’s water and crucial cooling capacity to its largest power plant.

In addition, Serbian Foreign Minister Marko Djurić and Albanian Prime Minister Edi Rama exchanged barbs on X, with the latter accusing Serbia of being in “a political bubble” and being in denial over the fact that “Serbia lost Kosova” long ago.

Kosovo was an Albanian-majority southern province of Serbia for most of the 20th century. Its people held broad political rights under socialist Yugoslavia until a decade-long Serb crackdown on dissent led to the armed conflict of 1998-99. A three-month NATO bombing campaign drove Serbian forces out and made the province a U.N. protectorate.

Kosovo declared independence in 2008 and, to date, it is recognized by over 100 nations, including the U.S., U.K. and 22 of the 27 EU member countries. It is also a potential EU candidate country, submitting its application in December 2022.

The country’s status has long been a favorite talking point for Russian President Vladimir Putin, who has used it to justify invading Georgia in 2008 and annexing Crimea in 2014. Kosovo’s Foreign Minister Glauk Konjufca said he took note of Zelenskyy’s views “with regret” and that such rhetoric echoes “Russia’s attempts to invoke Kosova as a precedent.”

As for why Ukraine’s leader would wade into the intractable Balkan issue at all, it likely comes down to weaponry.

World.title: Farage vs. Binface: Inside the Clacton by-election circus
World.content:
The feeling that the town has been made to look daft was apparent even among those preparing to vote once again to return the Reform UK leader to parliament. And it’s not the rival candidate wearing a trash can on his head that they’re holding responsible for the “farce.”

Thursday may not be the end of the matter, either. A parliamentary investigation into Farage’s alleged failure to declare millions of pounds of donations in the run-up to his 2024 election could mean yet another by-election — and a tougher battle for the right-wing populist next time around.

Bid for absolution

This self-inflicted campaign is taking place because of Farage’s decision to resign his parliamentary seat and put his fate in the hands of Clacton’s residents.

Ordinary punters, he argued, should be the ones to have their say as he faced mounting questions over undeclared donations. The gamble was that such a vote would absolve him of wrongdoing in the eyes of the public, regardless of the findings in two parliamentary probes — one over a £5 million donation from a crypto-entrepreneur, and the other into support from a convicted fraudster. Farage has denied wrongdoing in both instances, arguing that help was given in a personal capacity.

Farage speaks during a press conference on a plan to deport foreign prisoners, in London on Aug. 10, 2026. | Dan Kitwood/Getty Images

But Britain’s main political parties took one look at this ploy and opted out. That’s how Count Binface, one of the most enthusiastic inheritors of a rich British tradition of standing as a satirical candidate in elections, ended up as Farage’s most high-profile rival.

Others risking their £500 deposit to get their names on the 90-cm-long ballot paper include rival jokesters with names ranging from Howling Laud Hope, Nick the Incredible Flying Brick and Baron Von Thunderclap. Broadcast rules mean the 34-strong candidate list needs to be read in full at every mention of Farage’s by-election on TV.

World.title: Europe’s new border system is causing huge airport queues as EES wait times double
World.content:
Europe’s new border system is turning passport control into a serious headache, with peak queues at some of the continent’s busiest airports as much as doubling.

 

New data shows wait times have doubled at major hubs including Frankfurt, Amsterdam and Munich, as the Entry/Exit System (EES) scheme struggles to cope with the sheer number of non-EU passengers passing through.

Data shows that the biometric EES, which requires non-EU travellers to register fingerprints and facial scans, has seen queue sizes soar, as well as passengers missing flights.

The study by UK-based newspaper the Financial Times and travel analytics group Qsensor shows that in Frankfurt, the average wait time reached 120 minutes in July, up from 60 minutes the same month last year.

At Munich airport, waits are up to 60 minutes from 31 last year and, in Amsterdam, maximum waiting times have rocketed from 80 to 120 minutes in the same period.

While these times are shocking to see, it’s unpredictability which has made the situation so difficult.

Peak periods can mean queues of up to two hours, wait times are much shorter outside the busiest times.

Since the system was fully launched on 10 April, every traveller from outside the EU has been required to scan their passport and do a facial scan, as well as registering their fingerprints on the first occasion.

In practice, passengers have had to give fingerprints on multiple trips, due to glitches in the system.

EES kiosks have been malfunctioning and travellers have needed more assistance than operatives initially thought.

Related Europe has officially delayed the roll out of the ETIAS travel permit indefinitely

The chaos has drawn criticism from across the travel industry.

Ryanair’s chief executive Michael O’Leary poured scorn on the system, saying it had been “misdesigned”.

“Only the Europeans would invent sh*t like this,” he said in July, referring to the fact that his airline had witnessed large queues at some 15 airports across the continent.

Some airports have been deciding to temporarily turn off parts of the EES checks – including not collecting fingerprints during peak times – to ease the strain on passengers and workers.

That policy is due to come to an end in September, though – a fact which has seen eight EU member states and Switzerland ask the European Commission to extend it.

In a statement, the Commission says they are considering the possibility of continuing the practice.

“When it comes to the time after the summer, we are in close and constructive contact with those few member states where there are challenges at certain border crossing points,” a spokesperson said.

They added that EES wasn’t disastrous everywhere, and that registration takes an average of 70 seconds and that “in most cases” the impact on non-EU travellers has been limited.

World.title: The 'Musk effect' reaches Lerma: SpaceX books historic Burgos parador to watch eclipse
World.content:
"Will Elon Musk come?" The question has been echoing around the streets of Lerma for days, a picturesque village south of Burgos, in northern Spain. The arrival of SpaceX has transformed this town of just over 2,500 inhabitants, where residents, hoteliers and tourists are all looking towards the Parador, trying to work out what is happening behind its doors. The company founded by Musk booked it a year and a half ago to watch Wednesday's total solar eclipse from there.

 

Musk has ultimately not shown up, but the SpaceX effect is already being felt across the town: fully booked hotels, dozens of coaches and visitors arriving from different countries have shattered Lerma's usual calm and unleashed a level of excitement rarely seen in the town.

The cause of all this commotion is a total solar eclipse which on Wednesday will plunge some parts of Spain into darkness for nearly two minutes, an exceptional phenomenon not seen on the Iberian Peninsula for more than a century.

And SpaceX had been preparing for the event for some time. The aerospace company founded by Musk in 2002 booked the Parador in Lerma 18 months in advance to secure a prime vantage point from which to observe the phenomenon, right in the path of totality, with clear skies and little light pollution.

The hotel, a 17th-century ducal palace where Napoleon once spent the night, has closed its doors to the public these days to host a "private event". Inside, 140 US specialists are staying, including two professors from the University of Berkeley.

Is Musk in Lerma?

The possibility that Musk might appear in person spread like wildfire through the media and social networks in recent days. The buzz grew, fuelled by reports suggesting that the billionaire himself might travel to Lerma to witness the eclipse.

In the end, the COPE radio station has confirmed that Musk is not in the town. The guests at the Parador are technicians and eclipse enthusiasts and, according to the station, there is not a single celebrity among them.

His absence, however, has not stopped the entrepreneur's name being on everyone's lips among locals and visitors. The mere presence of SpaceX has been enough to put this small town in the province of Burgos at the centre of attention for a few days.

Lerma, like a rocket

The denial, however, has not slowed the economic impact. Accommodation in the area has filled up with the arrival of visitors drawn by the eclipse, while numerous towns along the path of totality are experiencing an exceptional influx.

The phenomenon goes far beyond a simple anecdote. Destinations lying in the path of totality, many of them small rural municipalities, are currently experiencing an extraordinary influx of visitors.

World.title: EU's centrist coalition might fall short of a majority for the first time
World.content:
European Parliament majority may not be a centrist coalition, according to new data.

 

The three parties — the centre-right European People's Party (EPP), the centrist Renew Europe, and the centre-left Socialists and Democrats (S&D) — which have formed a parliamentary majority since its creation would fail to secure one for the first time.

The seat projection was published on Wednesday by Europe Elects, an election data platform, which drew on voting intentions from each EU member state and modelled seat allocations based on each country's electoral law.

In recent years, Europe's mainstream political forces have been on a downward trajectory.

This latest projection marks a significant milestone: the centrist forces that have dominated European politics since the Second World War are, for the first time, projected to fall short of a majority at the EU level.

Parliamentary changes

The 2024 European Parliament elections already saw a significant shift in the political barycentre to the right, with right-of-centre parties gaining almost 60 MEPs, much of it driven by far-right, conservative and national-populist forces.

Europe Elects projects the S&D would suffer the largest loss, shedding 18 MEPs, followed by the EPP with 15 and Renew with nine. The Greens/EFA group, which has often propped up the parliamentary majority in the current term, would be further reduced, losing 14 seats.

Meanwhile, the hard-right Europe of Sovereign Nations (ESN) group, which includes Alternative for Germany, currently projected as the leading German party, would gain 19 seats.

The far-left group The Left is also projected to gain 19 seats, driven largely by leftist parties in France and Germany — a sign the political trend favours not just the right, but anti-establishment forces more broadly.

Still, most of the projected gains sit on the right of the chamber. Patriots for Europe (PfE), which includes Marine Le Pen's National Rally, is projected to gain 12 seats, driven by Spain's Vox and Austria's Freedom Party.

The European Conservatives and Reformists (ECR), dominated by Giorgia Meloni's Brothers of Italy, is due to remain largely stable, with three additional MEPs.

Group positioning

The hierarchy of political groups by size would largely hold, with the EPP remaining first, followed by the S&D, PfE, ECR and Renew. But the gap between the two main centrist forces and the largest right-wing group would narrow sharply, and Renew's position would be increasingly challenged by The Left.

The Greens/EFA group would slip behind The Left and the far-right ESN, becoming the smallest force in the Parliament — even as its votes become more pivotal than ever, since centrist parties would need the Greens more than at any point to form a majority.

One of the most significant shifts would occur within the EPP itself, where Spain's Popular Party and Poland's Civic Platform would become the largest national delegations, ending the German Christian Democratic Union's decade-long dominance of the group.

At the same time, the EPP would likely strengthen its position further, retaining the ability to form an alternative majority with right-wing parties, already a source of significant leverage for the centre-right group in day-to-day negotiations.

The ECR's standing could also be bolstered, having already gained significant institutional roles and legislative influence in the current term, potentially becoming more mainstream in the next.

Political trends

According to Europe Elects' director Tobias Gerhard Schminke, the latest projections confirm political trends that have defined the EU's electoral landscape in recent years.

"The first one that's often overlooked is that we see a fragmentation in the political system. So the EPP has about 21% support now in Europe. So, it will require a lot of political families to come together to form a majority," Gerhard Schminke told Euronews.

He also pointed to eroding support for the political centre, part of a broader decline in consensus around liberal democracy, human rights and cooperation between European states within the EU framework.

Another trend he noted is that within the radical-right camp, forces like Meloni's Brothers of Italy and Le Pen's National Rally have reached a plateau, while most growth is coming from the more extreme forces gathered under the ESN umbrella.

The next European Parliament elections are not due until June 2029, and three years is a long time in politics. Parliamentary groups can also shift before or after elections, which inevitably affects the distribution of power in the chamber.

Still, if these trends hold through the next elections, they would further test the EU's unwritten cordon sanitaire: the agreement among mainstream parties to keep extremist forces from power.

"What we still see is an incremental increase of the radical right camp overall. And we're now at the point where it is difficult to ignore these parties when it comes to coalition dynamics, be it in the European Parliament or at the national level," Gerhard Schminke said.

World.title: E-scooters  ‘public health challenge’ as number of injuries involving kids soared 15 times in UK
World.content:
The number of injuries involving e-scooters and children has increased more than fifteenfold in recent years, prompting doctors to call for regulation and public health communication, according to a study published on 11 August.

 

Researchers at the emergency department of Sheffield Children's Hospital, Royal Manchester Children’s Hospital and Alder Hey Children’s NHS Foundation Trust in Liverpool, United Kingdom (UK), analysed data from the three centres between January 2019 and December 2024.

During this period, the overall number of cases rose from fewer than 10 in 2019 to nearly 150 in 2024.

Of the 477 children treated at the three centres, 95% of the injuries were sustained by the rider, while 5% involved pedestrians.

The most common cause was a fall from the e-scooter, which accounted for 75% and nearly 11.5% were caused by a collision with a vehicle, while 5% involved pedestrians hit by an e-scooter.

Around one in four were head injuries and nearly one in five were facial injuries. But less than 2% of riders were reported to be wearing a helmet at the time of the incident.

The level of hospital care required for these injuries was substantial. 64.5% of the injured children required some form of imaging such as X-rays, computed tomography, or ultrasound scans. 13.5% were admitted while 7% required surgery.

The injured children were 12 years old on average, and nearly two-thirds were boys.

In the UK, there is no minimum age for using a private e-scooter on private land, while riders of rental e-scooters generally need to be at least 16 and hold a driving licence. However, 80% of incidents in the study involved a private e-scooter.

The study also pointed out that 74% of the injured children lived in areas of greatest social and economic disadvantage.

Researchers say children and teens are likely to be novice road users and to take more risks, and therefore road safety campaigns targeting them are needed.

“Utilising approaches like educational campaigns, such as bicycle safety schemes targeted to e-scooter riders, could be beneficial and have been shown to improve riders’ safety behaviour,” researchers wrote in the study.

Researchers view the surge in the number of injuries as a sign of an ‘emerging public health challenge’ and urge clearer public health messaging and a review of government legislation.

“There must be an onus on retailers to clearly advise customers of the law, and policymakers to regulate private e-scooters, such as with speed limiters, or mandate helmet use,” they wrote in the study.

“We urgently need to increase public and clinician awareness, have clearer public health messaging, and a review of government legislation to prevent further injuries and deaths,” they added

The findings come as governments and cities across Europe are reassessing how e-scooters should be regulated amid broader safety and public-space concerns.

On the day the study was published, the French capital Paris tightened rules on electric scooters and other rideables. In July, the German government proposed a bill to make rental companies such as Lime and Bolt directly liable for accidents involving their vehicles.

Madrid withdrew operators’ licences in 2024 over failures to control riding and parking.

Prague removed shared e-scooters from its streets in January 2026, and Brussels plans to follow in January 2027.

World.title: Feeling overwhelmed? These are the quietest countries in the world where you can truly switch off
World.content:
When was the last time you went somewhere truly quiet? We’re so used to the constant hum of cars passing by and neighbours talking loudly (or moving furniture, if they’re the upstairs kind) that it’s instantly noticeable when you visit a place that’s actually silent.

 

It’s… nice. Relaxing, even. We should seek silence out more.

Luckily for us, there’s a new Noise-Free Nations Index that reveals the quietest countries on earth where you can truly switch off.

Created by Go2Africa, the index was created using data points on population density, tourist density, rural land coverage, protected land, motor vehicle density, airport density, and train line density.

Across these indicators, each country was given a score out of 100, which was then combined to create an overall quiet score.

The quietest countries in the world

Bhutan came out on top, thanks to its rural land density, with more than 39,000 square kilometres of forested mountains, terraced valleys and highland terrain.

Plus, the Land of the Thunder Dragon keeps the amount of tourists who can visit low by charging a Sustainable Development Fee, making it one of the most expensive places in the world to visit.

Africa dominated the list, with more than half of the top 25 on the continent – including second to fifth place.

Namibia was the second quietest in the ranking, with just 3.83 people per square kilometre. The country is home to the Namib, the world’s oldest desert, and there are just 0.67 tourists per kilometre, too.

Third place went to Botswana, which, according to the travel operator, is thanks in part to its “low-volume, high-value” tourism strategy.

Rounding out the top five is Zambia and Gabon, with the former having one of the highest proportions of protected land in the world, and the latter being known for its pristine rainforest.

No country in Europe managed to crack the top 25, with the highest ranked nation being Estonia in 34th place, followed by Finland in 39th and Sweden in 40th.

This is due to the dense populations on the continent, high tourism inflow and expansive infrastructure networks.

The top 10 quietest countries globally

Bhutan – 89.44 quiet score Namibia – 86.69 quiet score Botswana – 80.86 quiet score Zambia – 80.64 quiet score Gabon – 80.61 quiet score Venezuela – 80.20 quiet score Chad – 79.82 quiet score Central African Republic – 78.18 quiet score Mongolia – 75.53 quiet score Bolivia – 75.40 quiet score

And the loudest

On the flip side of things, the loudest countries in the world list are dominated by Asian destinations.

Singapore took the top spot, as rural land covers just 30% of the island nation’s total area, and there are a whopping 23,609 tourists per square kilometre.

Somewhat surprisingly, the Maldives came in second place. While you’ll certainly find peace and quiet on the resort islands, the capital Malé is one of the most densely populated places in the world.

Barbados came in third place, with Go2Africa noting it has two airports serving such a small area, and frequent noise from cruise traffic, too.

World.title: Europe's scorching summer could cost EU economies €180 billion
World.content:
The prolonged heat gripping Europe this summer is on course to wipe out a year of economic growth, according to research published by Triodos Bank.

 

The analysis estimates that the damage caused by extreme heat and wildfires will cost a cumulative €180 billion in 2026, which represents around 1% of GDP. Against expected EU growth of roughly 1.1% this year, that would leave the bloc near stagnation.

The bank traces the damage through four channels, three quantified as EU averages.

Lower crop yields and dairy output, plus the food price rises that follow, account for about 0.15%.

Constrained nuclear, hydro and thermal generation, weaker solar efficiency and higher wholesale power prices add 0.12% to 0.15%, while disrupted rail, road and waterway capacity a further 0.15%.

The largest effect, and the hardest to pin down, is labour productivity.

Output per worker falls once temperatures pass roughly 25°C to 30°C, with the sharpest losses in outdoor and physically demanding jobs. Office work suffers too, partly because heat degrades sleep and cognition.

A cross-country analysis by Allianz, cited in the research, puts the loss at about 3% of output per hour worked for each degree above 30°C sustained over days.

France tops the table

The results are not a ranking of the hottest countries. Triodos scores each economy on the share of output in exposed sectors, commute times, air conditioning penetration and acclimatisation, then multiplies that by the excess hot days recorded this year.

France emerges as worst affected, losing an estimated 1.4 percentage points of growth, enough to tip it into a contraction of about 0.6% from an already weak starting point.

The Netherlands loses around 0.8 points, leaving it roughly flat. Spain and Italy have the most exposed workforces and the most hot days, but decades of adaptation blunt the impact of any single one.

Poland, with low air conditioning coverage and little acclimatisation, would be highly vulnerable but has had a cooler summer and should still grow by about 2.9%.

Costs that never reach the GDP figures

The human toll sits largely outside these numbers.

An estimated 20,400 heat-related deaths occurred across France, Germany, Spain and Italy during the June heatwave alone, and valuing the summer's roughly 25,000 deaths in life years lost implies a cost of €1.5 billion to €7 billion.

Wildfires had burned over 490,000 hectares across the EU by last week, against a 20-year average of 197,000 according to the European Forest Fire Information System, with France setting a record.

Lost ecosystem services from the area burned may add anywhere from €100 million to €4.6 billion.

Adaptation could cut productivity losses by around 40%, the research suggests, but not eliminate them, and its authors caution that their estimates rest on conservative assumptions.

The bank argues adaptation alone is not enough and Europe needs stronger action on emissions, pointing to the Commission's move on 17 July to ease the trajectory of its main carbon pricing scheme as the opposite approach.

World.title: Are you the travel planner of the group? You could win a free trip to Switzerland – itinerary included
World.content:
With great travel planning power comes great responsibility, but not always a vote of thanks…

 

Despite taking on the arduous role of mapping out spreadsheets, pinpointing a date that suits everyone’s calendar and creating a detailed itinerary, travel planners rarely get any credit for their efforts.

Now, new research from booking platform Klook, which surveyed 2,725 travellers across 10 countries, has found that travel planning ranks among the least thanked tasks people do for others.

The survey also found that for eight in 10 respondents, travel planning can take upwards of over 10 hours to organise a single trip.

And even handing over the reins doesn’t necessarily mean switching off, with 42% saying that even when someone else takes over planning, they continue quietly and anxiously monitoring the planning from the sidelines – ready to step in again at a moment’s notice.

Related Top tips and tricks for travelling internationally with young children

That’s why Klook is looking to reward those long-suffering planners with the launch of its global search for five traveller planners at their wit’s end from being unappreciated.

For those looking to be promoted to “pampered passengers,” Klook is offering a treat of a seven-day hosted trip to Switzerland.

"We built Klook to make travel planning simpler, so travellers can spend less time on admin and more time on experiences," said Marcus Yong, VP of Global Marketing at Klook. "Now we're taking that promise one step further with a fully-planned getaway for five travel planners who always get travel right for their friends and families.

"It's their turn to take a vacation from planning vacations," he added.

Do you know someone, or are you someone, who deserves to be relieved from their travel planning duties?

‘Thank You Travel Planners’ contest

This August, the search is on for travel planners that have tracked everything from bookings, backup plans and that one friend who hasn’t paid up yet, and are ready to travel planning-free so they can truly relax.

Five spaces are up for grabs on the seven-day VIP treatment to Switzerland this December, with round trip flights, premium accommodation and curated activities included – all preplanned and covered by Klook. Winners get to have a plus one accompany them, too.

Planners can nominate themselves or a fellow travel planner by submitting a summary of no more than 300 words detailing a trip they organised and the challenges they overcame while doing it.

Entrants must be at least 21 years old, hold a valid passport, be legally permitted to enter Switzerland and meet all necessary immigration or visa requirements, as well as be happy to share their journey on camera as part of Klook’s campaign.

The deadline to submit is 31 August, 2026.

World.title: Short on US Patriot missiles, Ukraine looks for alternatives
World.content:
Russia is putting pressure on Ukraine with ballistic missiles, but Kyiv is short of Patriot interceptors. Domestic production and European alternatives take time. Can Kyiv realistically reduce its dependence on the US?

Russia is increasingly relying on ballistic missiles for its attacks on Ukraine — precisely the weapons that Ukraine's armed forces depend heavily on Western support to ward off.

However, the crucial US-produced Patriot interceptor missiles are often in short supply.

How urgently does Ukraine need new Patriot missiles?

Extremely urgently. While Ukraine has set up a well-functioning defense network against drones, its armed forces are reaching their limits when it comes to fending off Iskander-M ballistic missiles. One of the few weapons capable of countering such missiles is, above all, the Patriot system with its PAC-3 interceptor missiles.

At the beginning of August, it became evident once again how patchy Ukraine's air defense has become. During a Russian attack on August 1, Ukraine could only intercept one of 27 ballistic missiles fired. President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said this was due to the fact that there were practically no more Patriot interceptor missiles left for the eight batteries stationed across Ukraine.

Three days later, according to Ukraine, Russia fired another 24 ballistic missiles as well as four Zircon hypersonic missiles, of which none were intercepted.

Ukraine faces Patriot missile shortage To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The French/Italian SAMP/T is considered an alternative to the Patriot system. However, Ukraine owns only a few of those, and the required Aster-30 interceptor missiles are also in short supply. In addition, the more powerful new-generation SAMP/T NG will only gradually become available. Therefore, the system is not a European short-term alternative to Patriot.

At the same time, Patriot deliveries are declining. According to Zelenskyy, Ukraine received only about one-third as many anti-aircraft missiles so far this year as it did in 2025. The war in the Middle East has further exacerbated the global shortage. Unlike at the beginning of the Ukraine war, the problem today lies less with launching facilities and more with Patriot ammunition.

What are the dimensions of Russia's missile capabilities?

Although exact Russian figures are not publicly available, there are numerous indications that Russia is ramping up its production. Moscow has, for example, significantly increased production of Iskander-M and Kinzhal ballistic and air-launched missiles. According to current estimates, it produces around 60 to 65 Iskander-M missiles per month alone, which amounts to more than 700 per year.

Reports indicate there are apparently shipments from North Korea as well. According to Ukraine, Pyongyang has supplied Russia with some 150 ballistic missiles since the end of 2023. In addition, a North Korean missile unit that has recently been deployed to Russia could be equipped with up to 120 additional missiles.

Ukraine calls on allies to help with air defenses To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

According to Ukraine's Defense Ministry, Russia launched 195 ballistic missiles of various types in July alone. Only 29 of them could be intercepted. Ukraine's military intelligence service estimates that Russia is currently capable of firing up to 100 ballistic missiles per month without depleting its stocks.

In contrast, US missile producer Lockheed Martin supplied only 620 modern PAC-3 MSE interceptor missiles worldwide in 2025. The company plans to increase its annual production capacity to 2,000 units, but only as part of a seven-year program.

Did the US allow Ukraine to build its own Patriots?

According to defense intelligence platform Army Recognition, an average of only some 133 Patriot interceptor missiles have been delivered to Ukraine per year since the start of the war. Given the intensity of Russian missile attacks this isn't much, which is why another option is gaining importance in Kyiv: domestic production.

In the wake of the NATO summit in Ankara in July, the Ukrainian government presented the matter as largely settled. Zelenskyy cited a political decision by US President Donald Trump to grant Ukraine licenses for the production of Patriot interceptor missiles. As recently as July 28, it was declared after a meeting of the two leaders in Washington that both presidents had had talks about the "implementation" of this decision.

Will there be a Patriot deal? Zelenskyy visited the White House in late July Image: Selenskyj/Telegram

Three days later, Trump caused confusion. The US had not yet approved Ukrainian production; it had to be "careful," Trump said, with this kind of technology transfer.

Nonetheless, the talks are continuing. According to information from Reuters news agency, American and Ukrainian representatives are considering, among other options, a model in which components are produced in Ukraine and missiles are initially assembled in Germany. Kyiv's participation in the production of a new, less expensive Patriot missile is also under discussion.

How quickly could Ukraine build Patriot missiles on its own?

Not fast enough to solve the current problem of overburdening. Outgoing Ukrainian ambassador in Washington, Olha Stefanishyna, estimated that setting up production of Patriot missiles in Ukraine was a process that could take anywhere from 12 months to five years.

A modern interceptor missile has numerous highly specialized components. A shortage of seeker heads, electronics or missile motors, for example, can limit the entire production. Until a domestic production is established, Kyiv is trying to obtain Patriot missiles more quickly. To this end, other customers are to pass on their shipments to Ukraine and get replacements at a later date.

What's the status of Ukraine's own developments?

Ukraine is no longer working alone on a system of its own, but is trying to set up a European-Ukrainian missile defense project instead. The program is known as Freya.

The core of the system will be the FP7.X interceptor missile provided by Ukrainian manufacturer Fire Point. According to the company's CTO, Iryna Terekh, its architecture is based on Soviet designs for the S-300 and S-400 air defense systems. Today's missile, however, had only some 20% in common with its predecessors, Terekh said.

Iryna Terekh, chief technical officer of Ukrainian arms manufacturer Fire Point, said the FP7.X interceptor missile is based on Soviet designs Image: Anna Pshemyska/DW

Now involved in the project are, according to Fire Point, more than a dozen European arms manufacturers. Their goal is to develop an interceptor missile costing less than €1 million ($1.15 million), which would make it less expensive than the modern Patriot PAC-3 missiles ($5 million).

However, this system will not be quickly available either. The Ukrainian side aims to have a prototype ready during the first half of 2027.

This article was originally written in German.

World.title: Europe braces for next heat wave
World.content:
More than half the continent, including much of Germany, is set for a third wave of extreme heat this summer. The prolonged hot weather has significantly worsened wildfires and drought conditions across Europe.

Millions of people across Europe on Wednesday were set for more extreme heat, as yet another heat wave descends on the world's fastest-warming continent.

In France, Italy and Spain, some 92 million people are expected to swelter in temperatures exceeding 35 degrees Celsius (95 degrees Fahrenheit) on Wednesday.

Some 300 million people — more than half Europe's population — will see temperatures pass 30 C.

France's firefighters on the wildfire frontline To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The new heat wave comes after Western Europe saw its warmest ever June-July period, the EU's Copernicus Climate Change Service (C3S) said on Monday.

According to C3S figures, temperatures in Europe are rising at twice the speed of other continents.

What temperatures are expected in Germany?

The German Weather Service has forecast highs on Wednesday of 34 C.

Temperatures are set to climb to 37 C on Thursday and as high as 39 C by Friday for much of western and southern Germany, the national meteorology agency said.

The looming heatwave is the third blast of extreme heat that Germany has seen this summer.

The prolonged heat has caused water levels on the Rhine to drop to record lows in some areas. The river is one of Europe's main waterways for transports of grain, minerals, fuel and other goods.

The drought conditions are impacting both Germany's environment as well as its economy, with companies that rely on goods normally transported via water suffering supply shortfalls.

France, Spain, Italy also brace for more heat

Extremely high temperatures of over 35 C are also forecast for France, Spain and Italy.

The latest blast of extreme heat comes just weeks after France and Spain faced some of the worst wildfires they have ever dealt with.

In Spain, where several wildfires are still active, the national weather agency AEMET is warning of temperatures of over 35 C.

Millions of people are flocking to the Iberian country to watch the total solar eclipse on Wednesday.

Spanish authorities are deploying over 33,000 law enforcement personnel to eclipse observation areas and access points, many of which are suffering from drought conditions.

Officials are working to prevent these gatherings leading to more wildfires being started, urging visitors not to light any fires, litter or park their vehicles in areas with dry vegetation.

"High temperatures, the accumulated dryness of vegetation, and the intense pressure on natural areas due to projected travel necessitate extreme preventive measures," Interior Minister Fernando Grande-Marlaska said.

Heat wave set to extend from Balkans to UK

The heat wave is also set to spread to parts of southeastern Europe, including in Greece, Albania and Croatia.

Tens of millions of people in the United Kingdom are also bracing for temperatures to climb over 30 C. The UK's Met Office said Tuesday that the country is expected to record its hottest-ever summer this year.

Several European countries, including Germany, France and Spain, have all set new temperature records this summer.

World.title: Germany news: Cabinet approves intelligence service reforms
World.content:
Published 08/12/2026 Published August 12, 2026 Interior minister hails 'new era' for Germany's secret services

Germany's Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt has praised newly approved measures that give the country's intelligence services new, broad powers.

The reforms, which we reported on earlier in blog, will give Germany's domestic and foreign intelligence services more scope in gathering and storing information and data, as well as operational powers to fight acts of sabotage and hacking attempts.

The German government says the reforms are needed to allow the country to better combat the growing threat from cyber and hybrid attacks, particularly – but not exclusively — from Russia.

"We are transforming our intelligence services ​into genuine secret services," Dobrindt told a press conference in Berlin on Wednesday, adding that the new measures, which include artificial intelligence tools, will "revolutionize Germany's security architecture."

Germany's intelligence services were set up after the end of World War II, when memories of the Nazi regime were still recent, while people in the former East Germany lived under the oppression and intense state surveillance of the notorious secret state police, known as the Stasi.

Because of that legacy, Dobrindt said Germany was "catching up with what is possible in other European countries" such as France or the UK, whose secret services have more and broader powers.

World.title: EU packaging rules: Why small firms are sounding the alarm
World.content:
The EU has introduced new rules targeting packaging waste and "forever chemicals." Although the changes will be phased in slowly, some small sellers have already paused shipments due to the additional red tape.

What changes from Wednesday?

In a drive to cut waste and improve public health, new European Union rules take effect on Wednesday, banning high levels of PFAS "forever chemicals" in packaging.

Under the EU's Packaging and Packaging Waste Regulation (PPWR), any new packaging products entering the market will now have to meet tighter standards if designed to come into contact with food.

PFAS have been linked to increased risks of certain cancers and other health conditions.

Although the amount of material people are exposed to from food packaging is usually low, scientists are worried about the long-term effects.

After all, PFAS are highly persistent chemicals and accumulate in the body and the environment.

PFAS are used to make paper and cardboard packaging both grease- and water-resistant and are found in everything from pizza boxes to TV dinners.

Packaging with lower PFAS reduces the risk of these persistent chemicals migrating into food or the natural world when thrown away.

The new rules are in addition to curbs on bisphenol A (BPA) in food-contact materials, which took effect across the EU last month.

Recycling rates in the EU are rising, but lower than the increase in packaging waste Image: Robert Michael/dpa/picture alliance

Under PPWR, businesses will not be required to recall or destroy packaging or goods that were already on the market before Wednesday.

While consumers won't notice any difference, businesses have fiercely criticized the changes, which also require packaging to meet new sustainability standards.

Are the new packaging rules too complicated?

Many small businesses and online traders believe the additional cost and red tape are too cumbersome.

They complain that they now have to register their packaging in multiple EU states, often with fees.

"Instead of facilitating cross-border trade, the new rules threaten to make it significantly more difficult," warned Händlerbund, the German online retailers' association.

Händlerbund warned its members : "There is no minimum quantity and no exception for small businesses."

EU lawmaker Elisabeth Dieringer of the far-right Freedom Party of Austria has warned that PPWR would mean five-figure costs for medium-sized firms.

"While corporations have their own departments for this [red tape], the Mittelstand [medium-sized firms] has little choice but to 'eat or die,'" she wrote on X on Tuesday.

Several businesses, from sole traders to medium-sized firms, said they had paused deliveries to and within the EU due to the new rules.

"Under these rules, I would need to appoint an authorized representative in every single EU country I send to," wrote the owner of a small online store, Monstaas Workshop, in an Instagram post.

"The cost is around €300 ($346) per country, per year ... these costs are simply not affordable."

From pollution to progress: Tackling PFAS across continents To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Swedish embedded electronic devices maker iLabs Electronics said it would halt web shop orders from EU countries.

"The cost and administrative burden [of PPWR] is now out of proportion to our direct sales volume," iLabs wrote on its website.

A petition on change.org had been signed by more than 45,000 people by Wednesday morning, calling on Brussels to "stop destroying EU micro-businesses."

How bad is the EU's packaging waste problem?

According to the European Commission, the bloc's executive arm, EU countries have witnessed a 20% increase in packaging waste over the last decade.

Without PPWR, Brussels says, discarded packaging was set to rise by another 19% by 2030, driven by the boom in online shopping and convenience food.

EU data shows that 178 kilograms (392 pounds) of packaging waste was generated per person across the bloc in 2023. Of this, 35.3 kg was plastic packaging, only 42% of which was recycled.

At 215 kg per capita (in 2023), Germany's waste from packaging is much higher than the EU average.

Scientists are worried about long-term exposure to 'forever chemicals' in food packaging Image: Tobias Steinmaurer/photosteinmaurer.com/IMAGO

Each EU resident generates the equivalent of roughly half a kilo of packaging waste every day, data from Eurostat, the EU's statistics agency, shows.

According to Brussels, the volume of waste has grown faster than recycling rates over the past decade.

Packaging also ⁠accounts ⁠for about 40% of plastic consumption in Europe, an EU official told reporters at a briefing on Tuesday.

What are the EU's long-term waste targets?

Although PFAS is the main focus of this initial phase of PPWR, the EU has set binding targets to cut packaging waste by 5% by 2030 and 15% by 2040.

From 2028, packaging manufacturers will be required to carry standardized labels that clearly show the materials used and how it should be recycled or disposed of.

Some stores, particularly restaurants and cafes, will be required to offer customers reusable packaging as an option, often at no extra charge.

Deposit-and-return schemes for plastic bottles and soda cans, such as those operational in Germany and the Netherlands, will be rolled out across the EU by 2029.

Then from 2030, all packaging placed on the EU market, including single-use plastic bottles, must be designed to be recyclable.

Packaging will also be required to be kept to a minimum to protect the product and fulfill its function.

This measure is meant to reduce the overuse of packaging for marketing purposes.

Meanwhile, single-use plastic packaging for fresh produce will be banned from 2030.

EU states will be able to set their own penalties for non-compliance, with German authorities allowed to impose fines of up to €200,000 ($230,000) for more serious breaches.

Edited by: Kristie Pladson

World.title: AI helping create popular mobile sports games
World.content:
After the World Cup and before the domestic season, many fans still crave more football. Amateur coders are helping to fill this gap.

After the World Cup and before the domestic football season begins, the world's most popular sport tends to enjoy a relatively quiet period. For some though, the need for football remains.

This summer that demand has been met by the creation of a raft of mobile sports games in which players can dive into nostalgia and storytelling. This craze has seemingly been inspired by the viral 82-0 basketball game in which players can draft an all-time NBA starting five by spinning a random wheel for teams and decades.

Inspired by this, Deniz Sancar, a hobbyist coder who works in advertising, created 38-0-0. Sancar told Mobilegamer.biz that despite having no previous coding experience, he built the game overnight with Claude Code, an advanced AI assistant that is designed to help with coding. The game was No. 1 in the UK App Store games charts in June.

Destiny Eleven: From TikTok to France and the world

Another example is Destiny Eleven. Maxence Pigne, a PSG fan and a project manager, was inspired by a game he saw on TikTok that allowed players to play out the career of a professional footballer. After the 2026 World Cup, Pigne released his version, also created with the help of AI assistant Claude, which took the original idea further by offering more variety and choices in the career.

The man who specializes in computer science told French weekly Le Point that the decision to publish the free game earlier than planned paid off because by the end of July, the game had over 1 million players with 14 million careers having been created. Leverkusen striker Martin Terrier is reportedly a fan of the game, which has seen many variations in different languages emerge in the weeks since its arrival.

Mobile games are big business

It's clear mobile games have come a long way since Nokia released "Snake" back in 1997. They are now big business. According to digital market intelligence platform Sensor Tower, approximately 50 billion mobile games were downloaded in 2025, generating $82 billion (€71 billion) in in-app purchases. According to Game, the German games industry association, revenue in Germany in 2025 was approximately $3.12 billion, with 28.1 million players.

"This clearly indicates that mobile gaming in Germany is no longer a niche topic, but rather a serious genre with significant purchasing power," Kyle Kuscu, chairman of the German Mobile Gaming Association, told DW.

"This is also relevant for the esports sector: Germany has a broad player base, and mobile gaming is the largest platform in the country in terms of user numbers."

This summer, the emergence of sports-drafting games has clearly benefited from a World Cup summer but also because of game design.

"The World Cup or tournament effect only amplifies this, but it doesn't fully explain the hype on its own," Kuscu said.

"Such games satisfy a fundamental human need shared by many users: control, optimization and imagination in a very compact format — in other words, the feeling of having it all in your own hands, of building the perfect team or career, without a long learning curve or complex controls."

What counts is the 'idea and final execution'

AI has been involved in video game creation for years, but with smarter and faster AI in 2026 comes an even more financially efficient approach for game developers. This is particularly important in the tough economic conditions in which free-to-play mobile games operate.

"The trend toward smaller, faster-to-develop games with AI support is likely to continue and may even grow. But I don't believe that every viral success story will be repeated," Kuscu said.

"Based on our own experience and confirmed by external sources, we know that AI has long been used extensively and intensively in game development, especially for coding, prototyping, research and repetitive tasks. At the same time, many people remain skeptical about quality, dependencies and creative limitations. Even if we advocate for the use of AI-assisted programming, what ultimately counts is the idea and the final execution of a game, and that won't change."

Short shelf life a key problem in a competitive market

The challenges for such games to maintain their success remains a major challenge though, especially given the overall gaming market remains a far from profitable industry. More teams can release more games, but that makes competition stiffer than ever.

"The biggest hurdle is no longer just production, but the business model behind it: Mobile games are extremely dependent on user attention, repeat usage, and, above all, in-app purchases," Kuscu said.

"A viral launch does not yet equate to a viable, let alone successful, business. They must get a handle on session duration, community building, update frequency and monetization very quickly. This is precisely where the crux of the matter lies, because otherwise the hype will fizzle out before the game can become a sustainable title."

Whether it's the immersive storytelling nature of these games or the ease with which a virtual world can be reached, it's clear that these games have found a gap in the market. History suggests they might not be popular for long, but even if this summer is their moment in the sun, their emergence appears a significant reminder of the challenges the mobile game industry will face with the increased involvement of AI.

Edited by: Chuck Penfold

World.title: Zambia's 2026 election: Key issues to watch
World.content:
Economic recovery, youth turnout, women's representation and judicial independence are among the issues shaping Zambia's vote on Thursday.

Zambia's general election on Thursday will be fought on economic recovery, governance reforms and a sweeping change to the country's parliamentary map.

Incumbent President Hakainde Hichilema, leader of the United Party for National Development (UPND), is seeking a second term against 14 opponents.

His principal challenger is Brian Mundubile, a former ally of the late President Edgar Lungu, who has surged to the front of a fragmented opposition after being backed by a coalition of rival parties.

The Electoral Commission announced in April that 70 new constituencies would be added, raising the number of parliamentary seats from 156 to 226, creating smaller, more local voting districts. Up to 8.7 million voters are expected to take part in the elections, a majority of whom are women.

Economic issues dominate Zambia's election campaign

Economic issues dominate voters' concerns. Official data shows that over 70% of the population lives on less than three dollars a day, and many households survive on salaries between $60 and $100 (€52 and €87) a month while grocery prices keep rising.

"I would like the new government to increase our salaries. [Maize meal] is very expensive. Everything is expensive," said security guard Lucky Mutelo.

Rebecca, a market shopper, echoes the sentiment, noting that "the cost of living is still too high."

Incumbent Hakainde Hichilema faces Brian Mundubile, a former ally of late president Edgar Lungu Image: Brian Mundubile media team

The government has been making significant gains on these issues.

Hichilema's government has secured a landmark debt restructuring agreement, restoring an International Monetary Fund program and supporting economic growth. Inflation fell to 6.5% in June this year.

The administration has also rolled out free education and an expanded Constituency Development Fund, which allocates public money directly to each of the country's constituencies to finance community-driven local development projects and infrastructure.

Nevertheless, a historic drought that crippled agriculture and forced severe hydro‑power load‑shedding has strained household finances.

Election demographics amid a fragmented electoral field

To become president, a candidate must secure 50% plus one of the total votes cast. If no contender reaches this threshold, the two highest‑scoring candidates will face off in a second round — a mechanism designed to ensure that the president enjoys a clear popular mandate.

There are 14 names on the ballot, so even small swings in support across the 10 provinces could determine whether the election goes to a second round.

Our time is now: Zambia's youth running in elections To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Analysts say the election's outcome would hinge on urban centers such as Lusaka and the Copperbelt, where cost‑of‑living pressures are most acute, while rural provinces traditionally follow established party loyalties.

Rural voters in the Southern, Western and North‑Western provinces historically back the UPND, whereas the opposition targets the Northern, Luapula and Eastern provinces.

Agence France-Presse (AFP) reported that the high youth turnout that propelled the current president Hakainde Hichilema to a landslide victory in 2021 is expected to be a decisive factor again, especially in densely populated urban districts.

Nearly half of registered voters are aged between 18 and 35, making young people a potentially pivotal bloc, Institute for Security Studies researcher Zenge Simakoloyi told AFP.

Can women swing Zambia's election?

Gender representation is another prominent theme. In this election, there is one female presidential candidate and four female running mates.

Mwaka Nyirenda is one of a handful of women contesting for a parliamentary seat.

"Politics is still a man's world. People doubt you, underestimate you and try to intimidate you," she told DW, noting that the financial bias still favors male candidates.

Women comprise roughly 51% of Zambia's population but hold only about 15% of parliamentary seats, and fewer than 20% of political leadership positions.

Leah Diana Mitaba, publicity secretary of the Non‑Governmental Coordinating Council, warns that these figures "demonstrate that Zambia remains far from achieving the 50:50 gender representation envisaged in the Constitution, the SADC Protocol on Gender and Development, the African Union Agenda 2063 and the UN Sustainable Development Goals."

Girls Gone Political, a civil‑society group, campaigns for greater female participation. Its leader, Dorothy Mtanga, thinks more civic education is needed. "There's the need for sustained democratic civic education to ensure that more women are elected into office," she said.

Judicial independence called into question

This election also raises questions about the independence of Zambia's judiciary.

Can Zambia trust election referee? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

In 2024, President Hichilema suspended three Constitutional Court judges who ruled in favor of his rival, former President Edgar Lungu.

Lawyer Linda Kasonde argued that "judicial independence is the ability to adjudicate on any matter, without fear or favor, regardless of the stakes involved in the case." In practice, opposition lawyers think the executive is trying to interfere with justice delivery.

Kasonde identifies two recent concerns. First, an executive‑approved salary increase for judges that bypassed the constitutional emoluments commission.

"The government increased salaries for judicial officers in 2025 outside the proper procedure, raising questions about whether the process was independent," she told DW.

Second, the appointment of 16 new judges in early 2026, many of whom hail from the incumbent's strongholds.

"These appointments call into question whether any decisions that will be made regarding the elections will be done independently," lawyer Kasonde concluded.

Amnesty International says Zambian laws, including the Public Order Act and cybercrime legislation, have been weaponized to restrict dissent, opposition gatherings and freedom of expression. It also warns that the increasing use of criminal charges against government critics could have a chilling effect on political expression.

Chief Justice Mumba Malila recently reassured the public.

"The judiciary stands ready to discharge its constitutional responsibility, independently, professionally and within the strict timelines established by the law," he said. Critics, however, maintain that true independence requires full structural and financial autonomy from the executive.

Continuity or change in Zambia?

Zambia's status as one of the region's stable multi‑party democracies in the Southern African Development Community (SADC) means that this election will influence regional democratic norms.

The country's ability to host a peaceful transition or renewal of power is a barometer for neighboring states, especially after recent defeats of incumbents in Botswana and Malawi.

Polls will be open from 6:00 a.m. to 6:00 p.m. Zambians will elect a president, National Assembly members, mayors, councilors, and council chairs.

This election holds the potential to either consolidate President Hichilema's reform agenda or usher in a new administration.

This article was compiled from several DW video reports covering Zambia's 2026 general election.

World.title: Solar eclipse: What to look forward to
World.content:
The last solar eclipse visible from the European mainland was in 1999. Here's what to expect, and how to prepare for this rare occasion.

On Wednesday, about 980 million people across parts of the Northern Hemisphere will have the chance to observe this upcoming solar eclipse.

They will be joined by hosts of researchers who will be taking advantage of the fleeting minutes when the sun's corona is visible from Earth to test specialized instruments and capture rare images. With them, they hope to gain a deeper appreciation of the material above the sun's surface .

What's going to happen?

During a solar eclipse, the moon orbits between Earth and the sun during the daytime, casting a shadow which temporarily darkens the sky and appears to blot out the sun. At the height of an eclipse, the moon's disk appears to align with the sun, revealing the sun's corona — its outermost atmosphere that flares outward like a crown (hence the name).

As the moon approaches and the sky darkens, you might also notice the temperature dropping, shadows appearing crescent-shaped, the wind beginning to shift and animals behaving unusually.

Eclipse fever sweeps Spain ahead of rare spectacle To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Solar panels will be able to produce less energy in this time. In Germany, this is expected to lead to a brief surge in electricity prices.

Right before the eclipse reaches its maximum point, known as totality, watch out for Baily's beads. These are the final rays of sun reaching Earth through valleys on the moon's surface. They appear as white specks encircling the moon like a string of pearls.

As night closes in during totality, keep an eye out for the stars that appear. Some might even be able to catch a glimpse of auroras or passing meteors.

Where will the eclipse occur?

If you live in Greenland, Iceland, northern Russia, northern Spain or northeastern Portugal, you're in luck! Viewers in these locations will be able to observe a total solar eclipse.

In most of Western Europe, as well as parts of northern Africa and northern America, astronomy enthusiasts will still be able to watch a partial solar eclipse.

And this is just the first of two eclipses in August. The second will take place on August 27-28, when Earth moves between the sun and the moon to create a lunar eclipse.

The next solar eclipse will happen February 2, 2027, over much of Africa, South America, as well as parts of Antarctica.

While eclipses themselves are fairly frequent occurrences, it's not that often that a total solar eclipse is visible on inhabited parts of the globe. The last solar eclipse visible for most of mainland Europe, for example, was in 1999.

What time is the eclipse happening?

The spectacle will begin at 15:34 GMT, with the moon slowly dimming the sun's light as it creeps into position. About two hours later, at 17:46 GMT, the eclipse will reach totality for about two minutes.

But where on the globe you are watching from will make a difference. While Icelanders will be able to observe the eclipse's totality at 17:48 GMT, viewers in Spain will have to wait until 18:27 for their chance.

Where can I watch the eclipse?

Since the eclipse is happening relatively late in the day, viewers are recommended to watch from high places to catch a good view of the sun as it dips toward the horizon. Most west-facing hills, towers and (safe) rooftops with an unobstructed view should do the trick.

If you're the kind who prefers crisper images, NASA is also offering a livestream .

Can I wear normal sunglasses to watch the eclipse?

In short, no. Looking directly into the sun can cause permanent damage to the retina at the back of your eye. Ordinary sunglasses, even polarized ones, are far too weak to provide enough protection.

Instead, you'll need certified ISO 12312-2 glasses, available at most pharmacies and opticians. Most are sold out already, but there are plenty of directions online for building a pinhole camera to safely watch the eclipse with small children.

You can also use a kitchen colander, or any other tool with small holes, to project tiny crescent-shaped shadows onto a safe surface.

Whether or not you are wearing eclipse glasses, never look at the sun through a camera, telescope or binoculars without a specialized filter, as the concentrated light can cause serious damage to your eyes.

Edited by: Martin Kuebler
